find walks a directory tree and, for every entry it encounters, tests it against the conditions you give and runs an action on the ones that pass. Its syntax looks alien at first because it is really a tiny expression language, but the shape is always the same:
find <where> <tests> <action>
find . -name "*.qmd"                  # by name, anywhere below here
find . -type f -name "*.png"          # regular files only (not directories)
find . -type d -name "images"         # directories named "images"
find . -size +1M                      # larger than 1 megabyte
find . -mtime -7                      # modified in the last 7 days
find . -name "*.tmp" -delete          # find and delete, in one pass

The Two Ways to Run a Command on Each File
find’s superpower is handing every matching file to another program. There are two idioms, and the difference is performance.
# One grep process PER file. The {} is the current file; \; ends the command.
find . -name "*.qmd" -exec grep -l "matrix" {} \;

# One grep process for MANY files. The + batches them into few invocations.
find . -name "*.qmd" -exec grep -l "matrix" {} +
With \;, find runs the command once per file, which is simple but slow across thousands of files. With +, find collects many filenames and passes them to a single command invocation, the same way you would type grep -l "matrix" a.qmd b.qmd c.qmd by hand. Prefer + when the command accepts multiple files.






Warningfind vs. glob: who recurses?



A shell glob like *.qmd only sees the current directory (and **/*.qmd in zsh for recursion). find recurses by default and works identically in every shell. When you need to reach into subdirectories portably, find is the dependable choice.

title: The Shell
text:
Editing a Stream

sed

grep selects lines; sed transforms them. The name is short for stream editor, and that is exactly what it is: it reads input one line at a time, applies an editing command to each, and writes the result out. Same line-at-a-time loop as grep, but instead of deciding whether to print a line, sed decides how to rewrite it. It edits a stream, not a file in place (unless you ask), which is what makes it a natural pipeline citizen.
You will use sed for one thing far more than any other: search and replace. The substitute command, s/old/new/, is the 90% case.
sed 's/old/new/'           # replace FIRST match on each line
sed 's/old/new/g'          # replace ALL matches on each line (g = global)
sed 's/old/new/gI'         # global, case-Insensitive
The s/// syntax is s, a delimiter, the pattern, the same delimiter, the replacement, the delimiter again, then optional flags. The delimiter is usually /, but it can be any character, which is the trick for editing paths without a thicket of backslashes:
# Replacing a path: / as delimiter forces escaping every slash
sed 's/\/usr\/local/\/opt/g'
# Use | as the delimiter instead and it reads cleanly
sed 's|/usr/local|/opt|g'

sed in a Pipe vs. In Place
By default sed writes to stdout, so it drops straight into a pipeline and never touches your files:
grep -r "TODO" . | sed 's/TODO/DONE/'    # transform the search output
cat config.txt | sed 's/debug/release/g'
To edit files in place, use -i. This is where a real portability wrinkle bites, and it is worth calling out because it catches everyone on macOS:
sed -i 's/old/new/g' file.txt        # GNU/Linux: edits file.txt in place
sed -i '' 's/old/new/g' file.txt     # BSD/macOS: -i REQUIRES an argument
                                     #            ('' = no backup suffix)
sed -i.bak 's/old/new/g' file.txt    # both: edit in place, keep file.txt.bak






Warningsed -i is not the same on macOS and Linux



GNU sed (Linux) treats -i as a standalone flag. BSD sed (macOS) requires an argument right after -i: the backup suffix, or '' for none. A script written on Linux with bare -i will fail cryptically on a Mac, and vice versa. When in doubt, sed -i.bak works on both and leaves you a backup.




A Few Other sed Tricks
Substitution is the bulk of it, but three more commands round out the daily kit:
sed -n '5p'             file.txt   # print ONLY line 5 (-n silences default printing)
sed -n '10,20p'         file.txt   # print lines 10 through 20
sed '/^#/d'             file.txt   # delete comment lines (those starting with #)
sed '/^$/d'             file.txt   # delete blank lines
The pattern is consistent: an optional address (a line number, a range, or a /regex/) followed by a command (p print, d delete, s substitute). sed applies the command to every line the address matches. That is the whole mental model.

title: The Shell
text:
Columns and Computation

awk

Where sed edits lines as text, awk understands them as records made of fields. By default it splits each line on whitespace into $1, $2, $3, and so on, with $0 being the whole line. The instant your data has columns, awk is the right tool, and it is shockingly capable: it is a complete little programming language with variables, arithmetic, and conditionals, not just a one-trick filter.
The grain of awk is pattern { action }: for each line, if the pattern matches, run the action. Omit the pattern and the action runs on every line; omit the action and matching lines are printed (so awk '/foo/' is a slower grep foo).
# Print the first column of each line (e.g. the PID from `ps`)
ps aux | awk '{print $1}'

# Print columns 1 and 5, in a different order
ls -l | awk '{print $5, $1}'

# Only rows where column 5 (file size) exceeds 1000
ls -l | awk '$5 > 1000 {print $9}'
That third example is the one that shows why awk earns its keep: $5 > 1000 is a real numeric comparison used as the pattern, and {print $9} is the action. You are filtering and projecting columns in a single expression, which would take a clumsier grep/cut combination otherwise.

Field Separators and Built-in Variables
The default split is on whitespace, but -F sets any delimiter, which is how awk reads /etc/passwd, CSVs, and other delimited data:
awk -F: '{print $1}' /etc/passwd     # usernames: split on : and take field 1
awk -F, '{print $2}' data.csv        # second column of a CSV
A handful of built-in variables make awk feel like a language rather than a filter:







Variable
Holds




$0
the entire current line


$1, $2, …
individual fields


NF
Number of Fields on this line


NR
Number of the Record (the line number so far)


FS
the input Field Separator (what -F sets)



awk '{print NF}'        file.txt   # how many fields on each line
awk 'NR==1 {print}'     file.txt   # print just the first line (a header)
awk '{print NR, $0}'    file.txt   # number every line, like `grep -n`
awk '{print $NF}'       file.txt   # $NF is the LAST field, however many there are
$NF deserves a moment: NF is a number, so $NF is “the field whose index is NF,” i.e. the last field. It is the idiomatic way to grab the last column when you do not know how many there are.


awk Can Accumulate
Because awk has variables that persist across lines, it can compute running totals, and the BEGIN/END blocks let you run setup and teardown. This is the feature that lifts it above the line-at-a-time tools:
# Sum the file sizes reported by `ls -l`
ls -l | awk '{total += $5} END {print total}'

# Average of the numbers in column 3
awk '{sum += $3; count++} END {print sum / count}' data.txt
total += $5 runs on every line, quietly accumulating; the END { } block runs once, after the last line, and prints the result. (BEGIN { }, its mirror, runs once before the first line, handy for printing a header or setting FS.) At this point awk has stopped being a filter and become a tiny report generator, which is exactly when to reach for it instead of stitching together five smaller tools.






Tipgrep, sed, awk: which one?



The three text tools divide cleanly along what they do to a line. grep decides whether to keep a line (select). sed rewrites a line (transform). awk treats a line as columns and can compute across them (analyze). When a task feels awkward in one, it is often because it belongs to another: filtering by a numeric column is awk, not grep; bulk find-and-replace is sed, not awk.

title: The Shell
text:
Composition Idioms
This is where the thesis pays off. None of the tools above is impressive alone. Their power is that they compose, and a handful of pipelines show up constantly once you start thinking in functions and streams. Read each one left to right as data flowing through transforms.

Count matches across a project
grep -r "TODO" . --include="*.qmd" | wc -l
grep emits one line per match; wc -l counts lines. Composition turns “search” into “count” with no new tool.


Find the most common values
grep -rho "la-[a-z]*\.qmd" . | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head
A classic four-stage idiom. grep -o extracts just the matched filenames, sort groups identical lines together, uniq -c collapses runs into counts, and the final sort -rn orders by count descending. This “sort | uniq -c | sort -rn” sequence is the shell’s GROUP BY ... ORDER BY COUNT.


Search inside a program’s output, not a file
ps aux | grep "[p]ython"
grep filtering ps is the canonical “is this running?” check. The [p] trick is a small joke that works: the regex [p]ython matches the text python, but the grep process’s own command line contains [p]ython, so grep does not match itself.


Edit a set of files chosen by content
grep -rl "old_name" . --include="*.qmd" | xargs sed -i '' 's/old_name/new_name/g'
grep -rl lists the files that contain the old name, and xargs feeds that list as arguments to sed, which does the replacement. xargs is the bridge that turns a stream of filenames (stdout) back into command arguments, the inverse of how a pipe normally works.






TipThe shape to internalize



Almost every shell task decomposes the same way: produce a stream (ls, find, grep, a program’s output), transform it through filters (grep, sort, uniq, cut, sed), and consume the result (wc, less, a redirect to a file, or xargs into another command). When a task feels hard, you are usually missing one of those three stages, not a fancier tool.

title: The Shell
text:
Gnarly Breakdowns

find in a Loop

The bulletproof way to iterate over files found by find, including files whose names contain spaces, tabs, newlines, or anything else.

find '<path>' -name "<filter>" -print0 | while IFS= read -r -d '' f
do
    # f is a row in the results of the `find` expression
    echo "$f"
done
This one earns its place in “Gnarly Breakdowns” because every piece of it exists to defend against a single enemy: filenames can contain almost any character. On a Unix filesystem the only two bytes forbidden in a filename are / (the path separator) and the null byte \0. Everything else is fair game: spaces, tabs, newlines, quotes, glob characters. A robust loop over filenames has to treat the filename as opaque bytes, and that constraint is what shapes every flag below.

The naive version, and why it breaks
The obvious thing to write is:
for f in $(find '<path>' -name "<filter>")   # don't do this
do
    echo "$f"
done
It reads beautifully and it is wrong. The problem is what $(...) does with the text find produces. Command substitution drops the output into the command line as unquoted text, and the shell then performs word splitting and glob expansion on it before for ever sees it.
Word splitting chops that text apart on every character in IFS, which by default is space, tab, and newline. So consider a single file named my report.txt. find prints it as the eight-character string my report.txt, but the shell splits it on the space into two words, and the loop runs twice: once with my and once with report.txt. Neither names a real file.






WarningTwo failures, not one



The $(find ...) approach has a second, sneakier bug. After word splitting, the shell runs filename expansion (globbing) on each word. If find turns up a file literally named *.c, that word gets expanded against the current directory and silently becomes the list of .c files there. Word splitting mangles names with whitespace; globbing mangles names containing *, ?, or [. The for ... in $(...) form is exposed to both.


You can partially rescue the naive loop by setting IFS=$'\n' so it splits only on newlines instead of spaces. That fixes filenames with spaces, but it still falls apart on the legal-but-evil filename that contains a newline, and it does nothing about globbing. There is no value of IFS that makes for f in $(...) fully safe, because newline is itself a legal filename character. We need a separator that is not a legal filename character. There is exactly one: the null byte.


Enter -print0
-print0 is a find action, the sibling of the default -print. Where -print writes each result followed by a newline, -print0 writes each result followed by a null byte (\0, an actual zero byte).
That single choice solves the unsolvable. Newline can appear inside a filename, so it cannot reliably mark the end of one. The null byte cannot appear inside a filename (it is one of the two forbidden bytes), so it is the one perfectly unambiguous delimiter. find ... -print0 produces a stream like:
./a.txt\0./my report.txt\0./weird\nname.txt\0
where each \0 is a real zero byte. The list is now parseable with zero ambiguity, no matter what the names contain. The convention is widespread: xargs -0, grep -z, sort -z, and cut -z all speak this same null-delimited dialect, which is why find -print0 | xargs -0 ... is such a common pairing.


Reading the stream back

while ... read

Now we need a consumer that respects null delimiters, and that rules out for. We pipe the stream into a while read loop instead. You have already seen read as the canonical line reader; here it is the same tool with two extra flags. Let’s take the loop header apart left to right:
while IFS= read -r -d '' f








Piece
What it does
Why it’s here




IFS=
Empties the field separator for this command only
Stops read from trimming leading/trailing whitespace, so spaced  .txt survives intact


read
Reads one record from stdin into a variable
The loop body runs once per record; read returns non-zero at end of stream, ending the loop


-r
“Raw” mode: do not treat backslash as an escape
A literal \ in a filename stays a \, not an escape sequence


-d ''
Set the record delimiter to the null byte
This is the keystone: it tells read to stop at \0 instead of at newline, matching -print0


f
The variable each record lands in
Inside the loop, "$f" is one complete, untouched filename



The -d '' flag is the half that pairs with -print0. read normally splits its input on newlines; -d overrides that delimiter. Bash strings can’t hold an actual null byte, so -d '' (an empty string) is the idiom the shell interprets as “delimit on \0.” Producer emits null-terminated records, consumer splits on null-terminated records: the two halves are matched, and a newline buried inside a filename now sails through as ordinary data.
The IFS= and -r here do exactly the job described earlier for plain line reading; read is doing the same work, just with a different delimiter. The only genuinely new ingredient compared to the everyday while IFS= read -r line loop is -d ''.






NoteQuote $f in the body



The breakdown’s example uses echo $f, but in real scripts write echo "$f" (and rm "$f", mv "$f" ..., and so on). An unquoted $f re-introduces the very word splitting and globbing this whole construction exists to avoid: the careful null-delimited reading is undone the moment you expand the variable bare. The quotes are the last link in the chain.




A subtlety

the pipe creates a subshell

One trap worth naming. Because the loop is on the right side of a |, it runs in a subshell. Any variable you set inside the loop (a counter, an accumulator) is lost when the loop ends, since the subshell’s environment doesn’t propagate back to the parent. If you need to keep state, use process substitution instead of a pipe, which keeps the loop in the current shell:
count=0
while IFS= read -r -d '' f
do
    count=$((count + 1))
done < <(find '<path>' -name "<filter>" -print0)
echo "$count files"   # the count survives
Note the redirect < <(...): the loop reads from a file descriptor fed by find, rather than being piped into. Same null-delimited contract, no subshell.






TipThe shape to internalize



find ... -print0 | while IFS= read -r -d '' f; do ...; done. Producer null-terminates with -print0; consumer splits on null with -d ''. It is verbose, but it is the only loop that is correct for every legal filename. When you need state to survive, swap the pipe for done < <(find ... -print0).

title: The Shell
text:
Writing Safe Shell

Shell rarely crashes; it obeys. That is precisely what makes it dangerous, and why a handful of defensive habits matter more than cleverness.

The breakdown above is a special case of a general truth: the shell’s failure modes are quiet. A C bug segfaults, a Rust bug refuses to compile, but a shell bug runs perfectly on your test directory and then silently does the wrong thing weeks later on an input you didn’t anticipate. The language won’t warn you; it just follows a word-splitting or globbing rule you forgot was in play. That is unnerving, and the right response is not to avoid shell but to aim your caution at the few places the sharp edges actually live. They are surprisingly few.

Quote every expansion
The single highest-leverage habit. An unquoted $var is subjected to word splitting and globbing; a quoted "$var" is passed through verbatim. This is the same mechanism that broke for f in $(find ...), and it bites everywhere variables appear.
rm $file        # splits on spaces, expands globs: a loaded gun
rm "$file"      # one argument, exactly as stored: safe

cp "$src" "$dst"            # quote both sides, always
echo "${args[@]}"          # quote array expansions too: "${arr[@]}"
If you do one thing differently after this notebook, make it this.


The shebang, and the promise it makes

The first line chooses your language.

A script is just a text file; something has to decide which interpreter runs it. That decision is made by the first two bytes. If a file begins with #!, the kernel reads the rest of that line as the path to an interpreter and executes it, handing your script’s path as an argument. ./build.sh with #!/bin/sh on top becomes /bin/sh ./build.sh. The name is a contraction of hash (#) and bang (!).
Two properties fall out of this that explain most shebang confusion:

The kernel needs an absolute path. It does not search $PATH. #!bash will not work; the line must name a real file such as /bin/bash.
It only applies when the script is executed directly. ./script.sh honors the shebang. bash script.sh ignores it completely, because you already named the interpreter. This is why a script with a wrong shebang can appear to work: everyone has been invoking it via bash script.sh.

The shebang is a promise about which dialect the file is written in. The two you will actually write:








Shebang
Means
Use when




#!/usr/bin/env bash
“this file is bash; give me bash”
scripts for machines you control (the common case)


#!/bin/sh
“this file is portable POSIX shell”
installers, CI, containers, anything widely deployed



#!/usr/bin/env bash is preferred over #!/bin/bash because it searches $PATH rather than hard-coding a location. On macOS, /bin/bash is bash 3.2 from 2007 (Apple froze it over a GPLv3 licensing objection), while a Homebrew bash 5 lives in /opt/homebrew/bin. env finds the modern one; the hard-coded path is stuck with the antique.






Warning#!/bin/sh is a promise, and nothing enforces it



#!/bin/sh declares POSIX, but which shell you actually get depends on the system, and none of them will hold you to the promise:

Debian and Ubuntu: /bin/sh is dash, a minimal POSIX shell. Bashisms fail here.
Alpine and most containers: BusyBox ash. Also minimal.
macOS: /bin/sh is bash 3.2 running in POSIX mode, and POSIX mode does not disable bash syntax. [[ ]], arrays, and <<< all still work.

The macOS case is the trap. Write #!/bin/sh, use [[ ]], and it runs perfectly on your laptop, then dies the moment it reaches a Debian CI runner or an Alpine image. Declaring sh gets you no local warning whatsoever. If you write #!/bin/sh, you must check the script with a tool (below); if you would rather not, declare bash honestly and use it freely.


Which to choose is a question about reach, not virtue. Personal scripts, repo tooling, and build helpers on known machines should say bash and use arrays, [[ ]], and <<< without guilt; POSIX costs real ergonomics and buys nothing if bash is always present. Reach for #!/bin/sh when the script must run somewhere you do not control: install scripts, container entrypoints, CI bootstrapping. The one genuinely bad option is claiming sh and writing bash anyway.


Checking POSIX compliance
Since no shell enforces the #!/bin/sh promise, two external tools do. They catch different things, so they complement rather than replace each other.
Run it under a strict shell. dash implements little beyond POSIX, so it rejects bashisms that bash-as-sh would wave through. This is a technique, not a feature: dash has no --posix or check flag, it simply fails on what it does not support.
dash ./script.sh        # bashisms surface as errors
Its limitation is that it is a runtime check. An unsupported command only fails if execution reaches it, so a [[ ]] inside an untaken branch goes unnoticed. Unsupported syntax like arr=(a b c) fails at parse time and is caught regardless.
Lint it statically. shellcheck -s sh reads the whole file without running it, so branch coverage is irrelevant, and it names each bashism with a rationale.
shellcheck -s sh ./script.sh    # -s sh forces POSIX rules regardless of shebang
Use ShellCheck as the primary check and dash as a confirming smoke test. Together they answer the question a container was the only obvious way to answer.






NoteWhat POSIX actually costs you



The features you give up under #!/bin/sh are the ones you reach for most: arrays, [[ ]] (use [ ]), <<< (use printf ... |), ${var,,} case conversion, $'...' escapes, and C-style for ((i=0;...)). Heredocs, $(...), parameter expansion, and functions are all POSIX and stay available. local is technically not POSIX but is implemented by every shell in practice, dash included, so it is a safe exception.




Fail loudly

set -euo pipefail

Put this at the top of every script. It converts the shell’s silent shrug into an immediate, visible stop, which is exactly the safety net your instinct is asking for.
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail








Flag
Effect
Without it




set -e
Exit the moment any command fails
The script charges past a failed step and runs the next one on bad state


set -u
Treat use of an unset variable as an error
A typo’d $flie quietly expands to the empty string


set -o pipefail
A pipeline fails if any stage fails, not just the last
grep x file \| sort reports success even when grep couldn’t open the file









Noteset -e is a blunt instrument



It is a real improvement, but it has well-known blind spots: it ignores failures inside most conditionals and command substitutions, and a command whose non-zero exit you expect (like grep finding no match) will halt the script unless you handle it, e.g. grep x file || true. Treat set -e as a strong default, not a guarantee, and still check the exit codes that matter.
Note also that -e and -u are POSIX but pipefail is not. In a #!/bin/sh script write set -eu and check pipeline stages yourself.




Know the anti-patterns by name
Most shell disasters are a small, recognizable set. Learn to flinch at these:

Unquoted $(...) in a for loop. The construction this whole section grew out of. Reach for find -print0 | while read -d '' instead.
Parsing ls. ls is for humans; its output is ambiguous and locale-dependent. Use a glob (for f in *.txt) or find for machine consumption.
Building command lines by string concatenation. cmd="rm $args"; $cmd re-runs splitting and globbing on the whole string. Use an array instead: cmd=(rm -- "$file"); "${cmd[@]}".
Forgetting --. A filename beginning with - is read as an option. rm -- "$file" tells the command “no more flags follow,” so -rf.txt is treated as a name, not a switch.



Let a linter retrain your instinct
shellcheck is the static analyzer the shell never shipped with. It catches the quoting, splitting, and set -e mistakes above automatically, and it explains why each one is a bug with a linked rationale. Run it on every script:
shellcheck myscript.sh
It is the fastest way to convert vague unease into concrete, named knowledge. After a few weeks of heeding it, the rules stop being a checklist and become reflex.


Verifying what you download

What a checksum actually proves, and what it does not.

Shell scripts install things, and installing means fetching a binary and running it. The ritual advice is “check the SHA-256.” Worth understanding what that defends against, because the usual explanation (catching corruption in transit) is the least of it: HTTPS already integrity-checks the wire, and a flipped bit fails the TLS record MAC long before any checksum sees it.
The real threat is that the file was already wrong before you downloaded it. TLS protects the channel, not the contents. It guarantees you received exactly the bytes the server sent; it says nothing about whether those bytes are the ones the author built. What can go wrong upstream:

Compromised distribution infrastructure. Someone reaches the release host, a CDN, or a package mirror and swaps the artifact. TLS delivers the tampered file with a perfectly valid padlock. This is not hypothetical: the Linux Mint ISO replacement (2016), the PHP git server compromise (2021), and the xz/liblzma backdoor (2024) were all of this shape.
A stolen maintainer account. A leaked release token uploads a malicious build to the legitimate release page. Nothing about the transport looks wrong, because nothing about it is wrong.
Mirrors and redistribution. Fetching from anywhere but the origin adds a party to trust. A checksum from the origin is what lets you use an untrusted mirror safely.

This leads to the distinction that makes the whole practice make sense. A checksum does two different jobs, and only one of them is about security:








Job
Defends against
Requires




Integrity
truncated or corrupt download, bad mirror
a hash from anywhere


Authenticity
tampered artifact, compromised host
a hash or signature from an independent path









WarningA checksum from the same page proves less than it looks



If you fetch the tarball and its advertised SHA-256 from the same server over the same connection, an attacker who can change one can change the other. Verifying that hash confirms your download completed intact. It does not establish that the artifact is genuine. The check is only as independent as the channel the hash arrived on.


Signatures are categorically stronger for exactly this reason. A GPG signature or Sigstore attestation is verified against a key you obtained previously and separately, so the trust anchor is not the download server. Compromising the host no longer suffices; the attacker needs the private key as well. That is a genuinely independent path, which a same-page checksum is not.
# Integrity: did the bytes arrive whole? (hash from the release page)
shasum -a 256 tool.tar.xz          # macOS; sha256sum on Linux

# Authenticity: was this signed by the key I already trust?
gpg --verify tool.tar.xz.asc tool.tar.xz
In practice the strongest check available is usually agreement across independent sources: if a distro package, the upstream release, and a checksum you obtained by another route all match, an attacker would have had to compromise several unrelated systems at once. That is a far higher bar than any single hash.






NoteWhat a package manager is actually buying you



The security value of apt, brew, or nix is not convenience, it is that they maintain that independent trust path on your behalf. Homebrew keeps artifact hashes in a git-versioned formula repository separate from upstream’s release host, so a silent upstream swap shows up as a mismatch. Installing by hand with curl | tar is a perfectly reasonable choice, but it is precisely that second path you are giving up, and doing the verification yourself is how you get it back.








TipThe safe-shell starting block



Every script: #!/usr/bin/env bash then set -euo pipefail. Every variable: "$quoted". Every script before you trust it: shellcheck. That trio neutralizes the large majority of shell bugs, which frees you to be relaxed about the 90% of shell that is genuinely safe, and sharp only where it counts.

title: The Shell
text:
Where to Go Next
This notebook is deliberately a core toolkit, not a complete reference. It covers the shell as a language and the text-processing tools you reach for hourly. The natural next steps, when you need them:

Scripting proper: functions, set -e/set -u for safety, argument parsing beyond $1, and traps. You already have the building blocks (variables, conditions, loops, the environment); this is about assembling them into robust programs.
awk as a language: this notebook covers the 90% (fields, patterns, BEGIN/END, accumulation), but awk has functions, arrays, and string operations that turn it into a genuine reporting tool when a one-liner outgrows itself.
xargs in depth: the workhorse for turning streams back into arguments, with control over batching and parallelism.

The one thing to carry out of here: think in streams of text and compositions of small functions. Every tool in this notebook is a function over text, and the pipe is how you wire them together.

title: Rust: Introduction
text:
Rust was created at Mozilla Research around 2010 and reached 1.0 in 2015. The motivation was straightforward and familiar to anyone who has debugged a segfault at 2am: systems programming is unsafe by default, and the traditional tools (C, C++) leave memory safety entirely to the programmer.
The designers asked a pointed question: can we have the performance of C with memory safety guaranteed at compile time, without a garbage collector?
The answer is Rust.




Rather than malloc/free or smart pointers bolted on after the fact, Rust builds ownership into the type system. The compiler tracks who owns what, and memory is freed automatically when the owner goes out of scope. No GC, no runtime overhead.



Instead of passing pointers around freely, Rust has a formal concept of borrowing — you can lend a reference to data without transferring ownership. The compiler (the borrow checker) enforces that references are always valid. No dangling pointers, no use-after-free.



Data races are a compile error. The same ownership rules that prevent memory bugs also make entire classes of concurrency bugs impossible.



Rust’s high-level features (iterators, generics, traits) compile down to the same machine code you’d write by hand. You don’t pay for what you don’t use — the same guarantee C++ makes, but delivered more consistently.



Rust rarely does things behind your back. Integer overflow is checked in debug builds and wraps in release (with explicit opt-in). Type coercions are almost never automatic. Mutability must be declared. This is intentionally more verbose than C++ in places, in exchange for fewer surprises.

title: Rust: Introduction
text:
Five Questions Answered
When the Tangerine and Passion Fruit Kombucha Genie popped out of my bottle, he said to me: “Five Questions from ye, I shall answer truthfully. But on Rust, from ye, they must be.”

1. Does Rust support Inheritance? If not, then why?
No. Rust deliberately omits implementation inheritance, and the omission is a design choice, not an oversight.
Inheritance bundles two distinct things: code reuse (sharing implementation) and subtype polymorphism (treating a derived type as its base). Object-oriented languages couple them; you inherit the implementation to get the polymorphism. Decades of experience showed that this coupling causes problems: fragile base class syndrome, deep hierarchies that are hard to reason about, and the pressure to contort a design to fit a tree when the real relationships form a graph.
Rust separates the two concerns cleanly. For code reuse, you use traits with default methods — a trait can provide a default implementation of any method, and any type that implements the trait gets that implementation for free (or overrides it). For subtype polymorphism, you use trait objects (dyn Trait), which let you write code that works over any type implementing a given trait. You can also compose behavior by having one struct hold another as a field and delegating to it, which is explicit and therefore more honest about what is actually happening.
The payoff is that Rust’s type system is simpler to reason about. There is no implicit behavior coming from somewhere up the hierarchy, and the borrow checker doesn’t have to contend with inherited mutable state. If you miss inheritance, you usually find that a trait with default methods plus composition covers the real need without the baggage.


2. Is Rust as efficient and fast as C?
Yes, with one qualification.
On the machine-code level, Rust and C compile to essentially identical output. Both use LLVM (Clang also uses LLVM), both have no runtime or garbage collector, and Rust’s abstractions — iterators, generics, closures — are zero-cost: they disappear at compile time. Benchmarks between idiomatic Rust and idiomatic C are routinely within a percent or two of each other, and Rust sometimes wins because the compiler can apply optimizations that would be illegal in C due to aliasing rules (restrict in C is opt-in; Rust’s ownership model gives the compiler that guarantee automatically).
The qualification: Rust has bounds-checked array indexing in debug builds. In optimized builds, those checks are often eliminated when the compiler can prove an access is in range, and idiomatic safe Rust often uses iterators or slice methods that compile down without per-access bounds checks. In tight inner loops over arrays this can still matter in some cases, and C has no such checks by default. If you truly need manual unchecked indexing, Rust gives you the escape hatch via unsafe, but you have to ask for it deliberately. In practice, for most systems code, the difference does not appear outside of microbenchmarks.


3. Is it possible for a Rust app to experience a segfault?
Yes, but it requires deliberate effort.
In safe Rust, a segfault is essentially impossible by construction. The borrow checker prevents dangling pointers, use-after-free, and out-of-bounds memory access at compile time. What you get instead of a segfault is a compile error. The few things that could cause memory problems at runtime (like out-of-bounds slice indexing) are caught and turned into a controlled panic rather than undefined behavior.
However, Rust has unsafe blocks, and unsafe suspends those guarantees. Code inside an unsafe block can dereference raw pointers, call C functions via FFI, and do other things the compiler cannot verify. Any of those can produce a segfault if you get them wrong. The critical design point is that unsafe is explicit and lexically scoped, so when something does go wrong you know exactly where to look: somewhere inside an unsafe block, not anywhere in the program.
So: pure safe Rust, no segfaults. Unsafe Rust, yes — but you opted in, and the surface area is small and visible.


4. What makes Rust good for systems development?
Systems code has two requirements that historically have been in tension: it must be fast and it must be correct. C and C++ solved the first problem and left the second largely to the programmer. Garbage-collected languages solved much of the second problem and compromised on the first. Rust’s central achievement is that it solves both at the same time, and it does it through the type system rather than through a runtime.
More concretely, the properties that matter for systems work:

No garbage collector. Rust is suitable for real-time systems, embedded targets, kernels, and anywhere else where GC pauses are unacceptable. Memory is freed deterministically when owners go out of scope.
Predictable performance. Zero-cost abstractions mean you can write high-level code without paying a runtime penalty. The performance model is transparent in the same way C’s is.
Memory safety without overhead. The borrow checker eliminates entire classes of bugs (use-after-free, buffer overflow, data races) at compile time. These are the bugs that dominate CVE lists for systems software.
Fearless concurrency. The ownership rules make data races a compile error. Writing multithreaded systems code in Rust is substantially less dangerous than in C.
unsafe as a controlled escape hatch. When you genuinely need to do something the type system cannot verify (MMIO, inline assembly, platform intrinsics), you can. The unsafe boundary is explicit, auditable, and doesn’t corrupt the surrounding safe code.
First-class C interoperability. Rust can call C functions and expose a C ABI, which means it can be dropped into existing systems incrementally rather than requiring a full rewrite.

The result is a language that can do everything C can do, on the same hardware, with the same performance characteristics, while ruling out at compile time the bugs that make systems code notoriously hard to ship safely.


5. Could you please compare Rust to Go, listing the pros and cons of each?
Rust and Go are both modern systems-adjacent languages that improve on C in terms of tooling and safety, but they aim at different targets and make very different tradeoffs.









Rust
Go




Memory model
Ownership; no GC
Garbage collected


Performance
C-level; fully predictable
Very fast; occasional GC pauses


Concurrency
Ownership enforces data-race freedom at compile time
CSP-style goroutines; runtime scheduler


Compilation
Slower (borrow checking, monomorphization)
Extremely fast


Learning curve
Steep; borrow checker requires a new mental model
Shallow; designed to be learnable in a day


Abstraction cost
Zero-cost (generics, iterators compile away)
Small runtime overhead (interfaces use dynamic dispatch)


Error handling
Result<T, E>; explicit, composable
Multiple return values; convention-based


Target use cases
Systems programming, embedded, WebAssembly, security-critical code
Network services, DevOps tooling, CLIs, cloud infrastructure



Rust pros: maximum performance, no GC, memory and thread safety by construction, rich type system (enums, traits, generics), excellent for safety-critical or resource-constrained environments.
Rust cons: steep learning curve, slower compile times, more boilerplate for simple tasks, the borrow checker fights you until the mental model clicks.
Go pros: fast to learn, extremely fast to compile, simple and readable, goroutines make concurrency approachable, excellent standard library for network and I/O work, easy to deploy (single static binary).
Go cons: garbage collector rules out hard real-time and most embedded targets, GC pauses are real (though small in modern Go), generics arrived late and are still maturing, less expressive type system, no way to enforce data-race freedom at compile time.
The practical heuristic: if you are writing a web service, a CLI tool, or infrastructure software where developer velocity matters more than squeezing every nanosecond, Go is faster to ship. If you are writing a database engine, an OS component, a codec, an embedded runtime, or anything where performance predictability or memory safety guarantees are non-negotiable, Rust is the better tool.

title: Rust: Introduction

Cheat Sheet

title: Rust: Introduction
text:
Project Anatomy
Three nested concepts organize Rust code: packages, crates, and modules. They map roughly — but not exactly — onto what you know from C and Python.






The Analogy Table
This used to be at the end of the Project Anatomy chapter. But by the time you get there, you no longer need it. So he picked himself up by his outer columns and moved shop.









Concept
C
Python
Rust




Distributable unit
.a / .so
Package (PyPI)
Crate (crates.io)


Project manifest
Makefile
pyproject.toml
Cargo.toml


Namespace / file unit
(file, no formal system)
Module (.py file)
Module (mod)


Import
#include
import
use


Package manager
(none built in)
pip
cargo





Crates
Before we define what a crate is, it’s important to understand what a fundamental unit of compilation is in Rust.

A compilation unit isn’t the smallest unit the compiler considers when compiling source. That is a syntactic unit. Rather it is the most granular unit the compiler creates when compiling code. For example, in C, a compilation unit is the object file (.o or .obj). But Rust is different.





The Rust compiler (rustc) does not compile individual files. Instead, it takes a single root file (like main.rs or lib.rs), automatically finds all the other files connected to it, and compiles that entire tree of files together in one single pass. And its output is either an executable (it has a main() function) or a library (it doesn’t have a main() function)

A crate is the fundamental unit of compilation, meaning it is the smallest unit of code that Rust will compile. The Rust compiler takes a crate and produces either an executable or a library. Think of it as the equivalent of a compiled C library (.a, .so) or a Python package on PyPI — the distributable unit that other projects depend on.
Two kinds of crates:

Binary crate — has a main() entry point, produces an executable. Root file is src/main.rs.
Library crate — no main(), produces a library for other code to use. Root file is src/lib.rs.





The Most Popular Crates
The following list is a top 30 crates capture from Most popular Rust Libraries. When I finish this document, I’m going to put it in a time-capsule bury it.

Packages
A package is what Cargo manages: a directory with a Cargo.toml manifest. A package contains at least one crate. Most projects you will work on are a single package with a single binary crate:
my_project/
├── Cargo.toml      # manifest: name, version, dependencies
├── Cargo.lock      # exact resolved dependency versions (commit this to git)
└── src/
    └── main.rs     # root of the binary crate
A library package has the same structure, but the crate root is src/lib.rs instead of src/main.rs. A package can contain both a main.rs and a lib.rs, producing a binary and a library from the same source tree.






Notelib.rs vs mod.rs?



They are the same in that they are both “roots” that define how code is organized, but they differ in scope:

lib.rs (Crate Root): The entry point for the entire library. It defines the top-level API exposed to external users and integration tests.
mod.rs (Module Root): The entry point for a sub-module located in a directory. It tells Rust that a folder (like src/commands/) is a module and manages the visibility of the files within that folder.

In modern Rust (since 2018), mod.rs is often replaced by a file with the same name as the folder (e.g., src/commands.rs instead of src/commands/mod.rs) to keep the file tree flatter, but their purpose remains identical.




Modules
A module is a namespace within a crate — the closest equivalent to a Python module. Modules organize code into logical units and control what is visible outside (pub) versus private. Items are private by default — you opt into visibility explicitly. Before we dive deep on our own, we are to share The Rust Programming Language’s “Modules Cheat Sheet”. It was just what I was looking for when learning about modules; so, here it is word for word:

Before we get to the details of modules and paths, here we provide a quick reference on how modules, paths, the use keyword, and the pub keyword work in the compiler, and how most developers organize their code. We’ll be going through examples of each of these rules throughout this chapter, but this is a great place to refer to as a reminder of how modules work.
Start from the crate root: When compiling a crate, the compiler first looks in the crate root file (usually src/lib.rs for a library crate or src/main.rs for a binary crate) for code to compile.
Declaring modules: In the crate root file, you can declare new modules; say you declare a “garden” module with mod garden;. The compiler will look for the module’s code in these places:

Inline, within curly brackets that replace the semicolon following mod garden
In the file src/garden.rs
In the file src/garden/mod.rs

Declaring submodules: In any file other than the crate root, you can declare submodules. For example, you might declare mod vegetables; in src/garden.rs. The compiler will look for the submodule’s code within the directory named for the parent module in these places:

Inline, directly following mod vegetables, within curly brackets instead of the semicolon
In the file src/garden/vegetables.rs
In the file src/garden/vegetables/mod.rs

Paths to code in modules: Once a module is part of your crate, you can refer to code in that module from anywhere else in that same crate, as long as the privacy rules allow, using the path to the code. For example, an Asparagus type in the garden vegetables module would be found at crate::garden::vegetables::Asparagus.
Private vs. public: Code within a module is private from its parent modules by default. To make a module public, declare it with pub mod instead of mod. To make items within a public module public as well, use pub before their declarations.
The use keyword Within a scope, the use keyword creates shortcuts to items to reduce repetition of long paths. In any scope that can refer to crate::garden:: vegetables::Asparagus, you can create a shortcut with use crate::garden:: vegetables::Asparagus; and from then on you only need to write Asparagus to make use of that type in the scope.
Here, we create a binary crate named backyard that illustrates these rules. The crate’s directory, also named backyard, contains these files and directories:
backyard
├── Cargo.lock
├── Cargo.toml
└── src
   ├── garden
   │ └── vegetables.rs
   ├── garden.rs
   └── main.rs
The crate root file in this case is src/main.rs, and it contains:
use crate::garden::vegetables::Asparagus;
pub mod garden;

fn main() {
    let plant = Asparagus {};
    println!("I'm growing {:?}!", plant);
}
The pub mod garden; line tells the compiler to include the code it finds in src/garden.rs, which is:
pub mod vegetables;
Here, pub mod vegetables means the code in src/garden/vegetables.rs is included too. That code is:
 #[derive(Debug)]
pub struct Asparagus {}
Now let’s get into the details of these rules and demonstrate them in action!


1. Inline
You can declare a module inline:
mod math {
    pub fn add(a: i32, b: i32) -> i32 { a + b }

    fn internal_helper() { }   // private: not accessible outside this module
}

// call it
math::add(1, 2);


2. File Based

Rust looks for src/math.rs

For larger code, modules live in their own files. Writing mod math; in main.rs tells Rust to look for the module’s code in src/math.rs:
src/
├── main.rs     ← contains: mod math;
└── math.rs     ← the math module


3. Directory Based

Rust looks for src/math/mod.rs

A module that has its own submodules gets a directory instead:
src/
├── main.rs
└── math/
    ├── mod.rs      # the math module root
    └── geometry.rs # submodule, accessed as math::geometry






WarningRauchen ist verboten



For cases 2 and 3, Rust decides which to use based on which file exists. You cannot have both src/math.rs and src/math/mod.rs.




Visibility
Four levels, from narrowest to widest:



Keyword
Visible to




(none)
Only code within the same module


pub(super)
The parent module only


pub(crate)
Anywhere within this crate, but not external users


pub
Everyone — including external users of the crate



// src/geometry/shapes.rs
pub struct Circle {
    pub radius: f64,        // visible to all
    center: Point,          // private — only code in this module can touch it
}

pub fn area(c: &Circle) -> f64 {
    std::f64::consts::PI * c.radius * c.radius
}

pub(crate) fn internal_check() { }  // crate-internal only


Submodules
A module can contain other modules. You declare them in the parent’s mod.rs the same way you declare top-level modules in main.rs:
// src/geometry/mod.rs
pub mod shapes;      // public submodule — accessible as geometry::shapes
pub mod transforms;  // public submodule — accessible as geometry::transforms
mod utils;           // private submodule — internal to geometry, invisible outside
You reference them with :::
use geometry::shapes::Circle;
use geometry::transforms::rotate;
Or fully qualified without use:
let c = geometry::shapes::Circle { radius: 5.0 };

This Hole is Deep
The nesting is arbitrarily deep. The directory layout mirrors the module tree at each level:
src/
├── main.rs
└── geometry/
    ├── mod.rs              # pub mod shapes; pub mod transforms;
    ├── shapes/
    │   ├── mod.rs          # pub mod circle; pub mod rectangle;
    │   ├── circle.rs       # geometry::shapes::circle
    │   └── rectangle.rs    # geometry::shapes::rectangle
    └── transforms.rs       # geometry::transforms
Each level follows the same rule: a mod.rs declares what is inside it, and child files or directories implement those submodules.



Spreading a Module’s API Across Files
The internal file structure does not have to match the public API. pub use re-exports items from submodules into the parent’s namespace, so callers see a flat surface regardless of how the code is organized internally:
// src/geometry/mod.rs
mod shapes;      // private — callers cannot reach geometry::shapes directly
mod transforms;  // private

// re-export selected items into geometry:: directly
pub use shapes::Circle;
pub use shapes::Rectangle;
pub use transforms::rotate;
Now from the outside:
use geometry::Circle;   // works — even though Circle lives in shapes.rs
use geometry::rotate;   // works — even though rotate lives in transforms.rs
The internal structure is hidden. The public surface of geometry looks like one flat module. This is how most published Rust libraries are organized: files and submodules for the authors’ benefit, pub use for a clean external interface.
mod.rs itself can also define things directly in the module’s namespace alongside its declarations:
// src/geometry/mod.rs
pub mod shapes;

// these live in geometry:: directly, not in any submodule
pub struct Point { pub x: f64, pub y: f64 }
pub fn origin() -> Point { Point { x: 0.0, y: 0.0 } }


Bringing Items Into Scope

use is your friend. Love him.

use is an extremely useful and flexible keyword that was described to me to an “alias injector”. The Rust Reference has the following to say about use:

A use declaration creates one or more local name bindings synonymous with some other path. Usually a use declaration is used to shorten the path required to refer to a module item. These declarations may appear in modules and blocks, usually at the top. A use declaration is also sometimes called an import, or, if it is public, a re-export.

It’s as if you are defining a root to which relative paths will resolve. Meanwhile the use of absolute paths are always an option. For example:
use geometry::shapes::Circle;

Circle::new(...);
Rust would be completely fine with the following:
geometry::shapes::Circle::new(...);

The thing I find the most cool about use is it’s flexibility. You may specify any portion of a full path and Rust will do the rest. use is essentially an alias injector: it binds a name at the current scope, and you can stop the path at any depth you like. Assuming that A:B:C:something exists, the following are all valid:
use A::B::C::something;

something();
use A::B;

C::something();
use A;

B::C::something();
I just went my pants. Very exciting indeed. And the architects did something that speaks on behalf of their thoroughness. It’s easier to demonstrate than it is to describe with words and hand puppets (🕺). Let’s assume that we have a module with the following hierarchy:
crate
└── network
    └── http
        ├── (functions/types defined directly in http)
        └── client  (a submodule)

Without self:
use network::http::client;

client::connect(...);       // ✅
http::get(...);             // ❌
network::http::get(...);    // ✅
You have: client, but you don’t have: http. You must write network::http:: to reach anything in it.


With self:
use network::http::{self, client};

client::connect(...};       // ✅
http::get(...);             // ✅
You have: http because self bound http itself. The self inside the braces refers to the module named at the end of the path before the ::{...}. So network::http::{self, client} is exactly equivalent to writing two separate use statements:
use network::http;
use network::http::client;


Superpowers and Conveniences
Finally, follows are some of the superpowers and conveniences built into use:

You can rename with as:
use A::B::C::something as do_the_thing;
do_the_thing()
You can pull in multiple items from the same path with braces:
use A::B::C::{something, another_thing};
You can combine both of the above:
use A::B::C::{something, another_thing as other};
You can use self inside braces to bring in the module itself alongside its children:
use A::B::{self, C};  // binds both B and B::C
You can glob-import everything public from a path:
use A::B::C::*;  // everything public in C lands in the current scope
Simultaneously binding a list of paths with a common prefix, using the brace syntax:
use a::b::{c, d, e::f, g::h::i};
Rebinding the target name as a new local name, using the syntax
use p::q::r as x;
This can also be used with the last two features:
use a::b::{self as ab, c as abc}


See Use declarations in The Rust Reference for more information.





External Dependencies
Dependencies from crates.io (Rust’s public registry, the equivalent of PyPI) go in Cargo.toml:
[dependencies]
serde = { version = "1.0", features = ["derive"] }
regex = "1.10"
Run cargo add regex from the command line and Cargo writes the entry for you. Then use it in code:
use regex::Regex;
This is the pip install + import of Rust, collapsed into one tool that also handles building, testing, and formatting.

Operator Overloading
Many operators can be overloaded by implementing traits from std::ops. For example:
use std::ops::Add;

struct Point { x: i32, y: i32 }

impl Add for Point {
    type Output = Point;

    fn add(self, other: Point) -> Point {
        Point {
            x: self.x + other.x,
            y: self.y + other.y,
        }
    }
}

let p1 = Point { x: 1, y: 2 };
let p2 = Point { x: 3, y: 4 };
let p3 = p1 + p2;  // uses our Add implementation
In the following table we include some of A listers and indicate the operator, the trait (in std::ops) and the method signature. For a complete list, see std::ops.



Operator
Trait
Method




+
Add
add(self, rhs: Rhs) -> Self


-
Sub
sub(self, rhs: Rhs) -> Self


*
Mul
mul(self, rhs: Rhs) -> Self


/
Div
div(self, rhs: Rhs) -> Self


%
Rem

PartialEq

<, >, <=, >=
PartialOrd
