title: Python Performance Analysis
text:
1. Introduction

“To make a rock’n’roll record, technology is the least important thing!”


1.1 Background and Motivation
The Python programming language, created by Guido van Rossum and first released in 1991, has experienced exponential growth in adoption over the past three decades. According to the TIOBE Index and various developer surveys, Python consistently ranks among the top programming languages worldwide, driven by its extensive ecosystem of libraries, clean syntax, and versatility across domains including web development, data science, machine learning, automation, and scientific computing. The language’s design philosophy, articulated in the Zen of Python, emphasizes code readability, simplicity, and explicitness, which has contributed to its reputation as an excellent language for both beginners and experienced developers seeking rapid prototyping capabilities.
However, this emphasis on developer experience and code clarity comes with inherent performance trade-offs. Python is fundamentally an interpreted language, meaning that source code is executed directly without prior compilation to machine code. While modern Python implementations incorporate compilation to bytecode, the overhead of interpretation remains a significant factor in execution speed. Numerous benchmark studies have demonstrated that pure Python code can execute 10 to 100 times slower than equivalent C code, depending on the nature of the computation. This performance gap has profound implications for computationally intensive applications and has motivated extensive research into optimization techniques and alternative implementation strategies.


1.2 Research Objectives and Scope
This research paper aims to provide a comprehensive, technically rigorous analysis of Python’s performance characteristics, suitable for advanced practitioners, system architects, and researchers seeking to understand the underlying mechanisms that influence Python’s execution speed. The primary objectives of this analysis include: first, examining the CPython interpreter architecture and its impact on performance, including the bytecode compilation pipeline and virtual machine execution model; second, investigating the Global Interpreter Lock, its design rationale, performance implications, and recent developments toward its removal; third, analyzing Python’s memory management system, encompassing reference counting and generational garbage collection; fourth, exploring performance optimization strategies, from algorithmic improvements to the use of specialized libraries; and fifth, providing a detailed examination of C extension development and Foreign Function Interface mechanisms for achieving near-native performance in performance-critical code paths.

title: Python Performance Analysis
text:
2. Python Interpreter Architecture

2.1 CPython

The Reference Implementation

CPython serves as the official and most widely used implementation of the Python programming language. Written in C, CPython provides the reference specification for the language and defines the Application Binary Interface (ABI) that third-party extensions must conform to. Understanding CPython’s architecture is essential for comprehending Python’s performance characteristics, as design decisions at the interpreter level directly impact execution speed, memory consumption, and concurrency capabilities. The CPython interpreter follows a traditional interpreter architecture with several distinct phases: lexical analysis and parsing, abstract syntax tree (AST) generation, bytecode compilation, and bytecode execution by the Python Virtual Machine (PVM).
The compilation process in Python differs from traditional compiled languages in that it occurs at runtime rather than as a separate build step. When a Python module is imported or executed, the interpreter first parses the source code into an Abstract Syntax Tree, which represents the hierarchical structure of the program. This AST is then compiled into bytecode, a lower-level representation consisting of operation codes (opcodes) that the virtual machine can execute. The bytecode is stored in .pyc files, which enable faster subsequent imports by skipping the compilation phase. This approach represents a compromise between the flexibility of interpretation and the efficiency of compilation, though it introduces overhead compared to ahead-of-time compilation used in languages like C++ or Rust.


2.2 Bytecode and the Python Virtual Machine
The Python Virtual Machine (PVM) represents the runtime engine responsible for executing compiled bytecode. Unlike hardware processors that execute machine code directly, the PVM is a software-based virtual processor that interprets bytecode instructions sequentially. The core execution loop in CPython is implemented in the ceval.c source file, containing a large switch statement that dispatches each opcode to its corresponding handler function. This dispatch mechanism, while straightforward and maintainable, introduces significant overhead compared to direct machine code execution, as each Python instruction requires multiple native CPU instructions to decode and dispatch.
The bytecode instruction set in Python is stack-based, meaning that operands are pushed onto an evaluation stack, operations consume operands from the stack, and results are pushed back onto the stack. This design simplifies the implementation of the virtual machine but introduces additional overhead compared to register-based architectures. For example, a simple addition operation in Python bytecode requires three instructions: loading the first operand, loading the second operand, and performing the addition. In contrast, a register-based architecture might encode all three operations in a single instruction. The stack-based design also necessitates additional memory operations, as values must be repeatedly pushed and popped from the evaluation stack.
Recent versions of Python have introduced optimizations to the bytecode execution engine. Python 3.11 implemented a specialized adaptive interpreter that generates specialized bytecode for frequently executed code paths, a technique known as quickening. When the interpreter detects that a particular code location is executed repeatedly, it may replace generic opcodes with specialized versions that make assumptions about the types of operands, enabling faster execution. For instance, a generic binary add operation might be replaced with a specialized version optimized for integer addition. If the assumptions prove incorrect, the interpreter falls back to the generic implementation. This adaptive optimization approach draws inspiration from just-in-time (JIT) compilation techniques used in other language implementations, though Python’s approach remains fundamentally interpretive.


2.3 Dynamic Typing and Object Model Overhead
Python’s dynamic type system represents one of the most significant factors contributing to its performance characteristics. In statically typed languages like C or Java, the type of each variable is known at compile time, enabling the compiler to generate optimized machine code that operates directly on raw data values. Python, conversely, employs dynamic typing where variables are references to objects, and the type of a variable is determined at runtime. Every value in Python is an object, encapsulated within a PyObject structure that contains a reference count and a pointer to a type object. This uniform object model provides tremendous flexibility but introduces substantial overhead for every operation.
Consider the seemingly simple operation of adding two integers in Python. In C, this operation compiles to a single CPU instruction operating on registers. In Python, the addition operator triggers a method lookup on the type object, which may involve multiple pointer dereferences and function calls. The actual addition must handle Python’s arbitrary-precision integer semantics, as integers in Python can grow beyond the limits of machine word sizes. Memory must be allocated for the result, reference counts must be updated, and type checks must be performed. This complexity transforms a single machine instruction into potentially hundreds of native operations. The overhead is particularly pronounced for operations on primitive types, where the semantic gap between Python’s abstractions and the underlying hardware is largest.

title: Python Performance Analysis
text:
3. The Global Interpreter Lock

GIL


3.1 Design Rationale and Implementation
The Global Interpreter Lock is perhaps the most discussed and debated aspect of Python’s architecture. The GIL is a mutex that protects access to Python objects, preventing multiple native threads from executing Python bytecode simultaneously. While this design decision has significant implications for multi-threaded Python programs, understanding its rationale requires examining the historical context and the technical challenges it addresses. The GIL was introduced in CPython’s early development to simplify memory management and maintain consistency with C extension modules. Python’s primary memory management mechanism is reference counting, which requires atomic operations to update reference counts when objects are shared across threads. Without a global lock, ensuring thread-safety for every object operation would require fine-grained locking at the object level, introducing substantial complexity and potential performance degradation from lock contention.
The GIL simplifies the implementation by ensuring that only one thread executes Python code at any given time. This guarantee means that reference count updates and other internal operations do not require additional synchronization, as the GIL provides the necessary mutual exclusion. The trade-off is that multi-threaded Python programs cannot achieve true parallelism for CPU-bound tasks, as threads must acquire the GIL before executing any Python code. The GIL is released during I/O operations and when executing certain C extension functions that explicitly release it, enabling concurrent I/O-bound operations. However, for CPU-intensive workloads, the GIL effectively serializes execution across threads, potentially making multi-threaded programs slower than single-threaded alternatives due to the overhead of context switching and lock management.


3.2 Performance Implications
The performance impact of the GIL depends critically on the nature of the workload. For I/O-bound applications, such as web servers or network clients, the GIL has minimal impact because threads spend most of their time waiting for I/O operations, during which the GIL is released. Multiple threads can effectively overlap I/O operations, achieving concurrency despite the GIL’s restrictions. This explains why Python remains popular for web development and network programming, where the ability to handle many concurrent connections is more important than raw CPU throughput. Frameworks like asyncio leverage this characteristic by using cooperative multitasking within a single thread, avoiding GIL contention entirely.
CPU-bound workloads present a fundamentally different challenge. When multiple threads compete for CPU time to perform computations, the GIL becomes a bottleneck. Each thread must periodically acquire the GIL to execute Python bytecode, and contention for the lock introduces overhead. The interpreter periodically forces threads to release the GIL after a certain number of bytecode instructions or time interval, allowing other threads to run. However, this context switching mechanism can lead to priority inversion and other scheduling inefficiencies. In extreme cases, a multi-threaded CPU-bound Python program may execute slower than an equivalent single-threaded program, as the overhead of lock management and context switching outweighs any benefit from parallelism.


3.3 Workarounds and the Path Forward
Several strategies have emerged for working around GIL limitations. The most common approach is to use multiprocessing instead of multithreading for CPU-bound tasks. Python’s multiprocessing module creates separate Python processes, each with its own interpreter instance and GIL. This approach enables true parallelism, as each process runs independently, but introduces overhead from inter-process communication and memory duplication. For workloads that can be parallelized with minimal communication between workers, multiprocessing provides an effective solution. Libraries like concurrent.futures provide high-level abstractions that simplify the choice between threads and processes based on the nature of the workload.
A landmark development in Python’s evolution is PEP 703, accepted in 2023, which proposes making the GIL optional in CPython. This effort, building on years of experimental work, aims to provide a free-threaded mode where the GIL can be disabled, enabling true multi-threaded parallelism. The implementation requires substantial changes to CPython’s internals, including replacing the reference counting mechanism with one that supports atomic operations without a global lock. The transition is planned to be gradual, with the free-threaded build becoming a supported option in Python 3.13 and potentially becoming the default in future releases. This development represents one of the most significant architectural changes in Python’s history and promises to reshape the landscape for multi-threaded Python applications.

title: Python Performance Analysis
text:
4. Memory Management in Python

4.1 Reference Counting
Python employs a hybrid memory management strategy combining reference counting with generational garbage collection. Reference counting serves as the primary mechanism for memory reclamation, where each Python object maintains a count of references pointing to it. When a reference is created, the count is incremented; when a reference is destroyed or reassigned, the count is decremented. When the reference count reaches zero, the object’s memory is immediately deallocated. This approach offers several advantages: memory is reclaimed promptly when objects become unreachable, the overhead is distributed across program execution rather than concentrated in garbage collection pauses, and destructors (implemented via __del__ methods) are called in a deterministic manner.
However, reference counting alone cannot handle cyclic references, where objects reference each other in a way that prevents reference counts from reaching zero. Consider two objects that reference each other: even if no external references exist, their mutual references maintain non-zero counts indefinitely. To address this limitation, Python implements a supplemental garbage collector that periodically identifies and collects reference cycles. This garbage collector uses a generational approach based on the observation that most objects have short lifetimes, while objects that survive initial collection tend to persist longer. The garbage collector maintains three generations, with newly created objects placed in the youngest generation and promoted to older generations as they survive collection cycles.


4.2 Memory Allocation Strategies
CPython implements custom memory allocators optimized for its allocation patterns. The primary allocator, PyMalloc, manages small allocations (under 512 bytes) using a slab allocation strategy. Small objects are allocated from pools of fixed-size blocks, reducing fragmentation and improving allocation speed. Larger allocations are delegated to the system’s malloc implementation. This tiered approach balances the need for efficient small object allocation (which is common in Python due to its object-oriented nature) with the simplicity of using system allocation for larger blocks. The memory allocator also maintains arenas, large contiguous memory regions from which pools are allocated, reducing the number of system calls required for memory management.
The overhead of Python’s object model has significant implications for memory usage. Every Python object carries metadata including the reference count, type pointer, and potentially additional fields for specific object types. A simple integer in Python 3 requires at least 28 bytes on 64-bit systems, compared to 4 or 8 bytes for a native integer in C. This overhead accumulates rapidly when dealing with large collections of small objects. Lists, dictionaries, and other container types add additional overhead for their internal data structures. For memory-intensive applications, these overheads can result in memory consumption several times larger than equivalent data structures in lower-level languages, potentially triggering garbage collection more frequently and impacting performance.

title: Python Performance Analysis
section: 5. C Extensions and Foreign Function Interface
text:
5. C Extensions and Foreign Function Interface

5.1 The Rationale for Native Extensions
While Python’s design prioritizes developer productivity, there are numerous scenarios where the performance gap between Python and native code becomes a critical concern. Compute-intensive algorithms, real-time processing requirements, and integration with existing C/C++ libraries all motivate the development of native extensions. Python provides multiple mechanisms for interfacing with native code, each offering different trade-offs between performance, ease of development, and portability. Understanding these options enables developers to select the appropriate approach for their specific requirements and achieve near-native performance where it matters most.
The benefits of writing native extensions extend beyond raw execution speed. Native code can bypass Python’s object model overhead, operating directly on primitive data types. Extensions can release the GIL during computation, enabling true parallelism in multi-threaded contexts. They provide access to hardware-specific features like SIMD instructions, which are essential for numerical computing performance. Native extensions can also wrap existing C/C++ libraries, enabling Python applications to leverage decades of optimized code in domains ranging from linear algebra to computer vision. Many of Python’s most performant libraries, including NumPy, Pandas, and TensorFlow, are implemented as C extensions, demonstrating the effectiveness of this approach.


5.2 Python C API
The Python C API provides the lowest-level and most direct mechanism for extending Python with native code. This API exposes the internal structures and functions used by the interpreter itself, enabling extension modules to manipulate Python objects, call Python functions, and define new types. Extensions written using the C API compile to shared libraries that are imported like regular Python modules. The C API offers maximum control and performance, as extension code can access internal object representations and bypass Python-level abstractions when appropriate. However, this power comes with complexity: developers must manually manage reference counts, handle exceptions through return value checking, and work with CPython’s internal conventions.
A simple C extension function demonstrates the mechanics involved. The function must accept PyObject* arguments, check their types, extract C values, perform computation, construct a result PyObject, and return it. Error handling requires setting an exception and returning NULL. Reference counting must be managed carefully: borrowed references must not be decremented, while new references must eventually be released. The module initialization code defines the module’s methods and metadata. While verbose, this approach provides complete control and enables sophisticated optimizations. The NumPy library exemplifies the potential of this approach, providing array operations that execute at near-C speeds by operating on contiguous memory buffers with minimal Python overhead.


5.3 ctypes and cffi
For simpler integration scenarios, Python provides ctypes and cffi as higher-level alternatives to the C API. ctypes is part of Python’s standard library and enables calling functions from shared libraries without writing C code. It uses foreign function interface (FFI) mechanisms to dynamically invoke native functions, handling type conversions between Python and C types. ctypes is straightforward to use for simple interfaces but incurs significant overhead due to its dynamic nature. Each function call involves type checking, data conversion, and libffi dispatch, making ctypes suitable for occasional calls to native libraries but less appropriate for performance-critical inner loops.
cffi represents an evolution of the FFI concept, offering improved performance and flexibility compared to ctypes. cffi allows developers to declare C function signatures and types directly in Python code, with the interface compiled to extension modules for efficient dispatch. The API mode of cffi generates C code that is compiled into an extension, providing performance comparable to hand-written C extensions for the binding layer. The ABI mode, similar to ctypes, uses dynamic invocation but with a cleaner interface. cffi has become the preferred FFI mechanism for many projects, offering a good balance between ease of use and performance. It is particularly well-suited for wrapping existing C libraries where writing dedicated extensions would be impractical.


5.4 Cython

A Hybrid Approach

Cython occupies a unique position in Python’s extension ecosystem, providing a programming language that extends Python with C-like features. Cython code resembles Python but can include type declarations that enable compilation to efficient C code. Variables can be declared with C types, avoiding Python object overhead for performance-critical computations. Functions can be declared as cdef (C-only, not visible from Python) or cpdef (callable from both Python and C), allowing fine-grained control over the interface. Cython also supports direct integration with C libraries, making it suitable both for optimizing Python code and wrapping external libraries.
The power of Cython lies in its gradual optimization approach. Developers can start with pure Python code and incrementally add type annotations to critical sections, achieving performance improvements with minimal code changes. Cython’s typed memoryviews provide efficient access to NumPy arrays without the overhead of Python object operations. The nogil context manager allows code to execute without the GIL, enabling true parallelism when combined with threading or OpenMP. Many scientific Python libraries use Cython to achieve high performance while maintaining readable, maintainable code. The ability to profile Python code, identify hotspots, and selectively optimize them with Cython type declarations provides an effective workflow for achieving production-quality performance.


5.5 pybind11 for C++ Integration
For projects targeting C++ rather than C, pybind11 has emerged as the dominant solution for creating Python bindings. Built on modern C++ template metaprogramming techniques, pybind11 provides an intuitive interface for exposing C++ classes, functions, and data structures to Python. Unlike its predecessor Boost.Python, pybind11 is header-only and has minimal dependencies, simplifying build configuration. The library automatically handles type conversions, exception translation, and reference management, significantly reducing boilerplate compared to the raw C API. pybind11 supports advanced C++ features including lambda functions, smart pointers, and move semantics, enabling seamless integration of modern C++ code with Python.
The performance characteristics of pybind11 bindings approach those of hand-written C extensions, as the library generates efficient wrapper code at compile time through template instantiation. Overhead is limited to type conversion at the Python-C++ boundary, which is comparable to other extension mechanisms. pybind11’s support for NumPy array buffers enables efficient data exchange for numerical computing applications. The library’s active development and widespread adoption in projects like PyTorch and TensorFlow testify to its production readiness. For organizations with existing C++ codebases or requirements for modern C++ features, pybind11 represents the recommended approach for Python integration.

title: Python Performance Analysis
text:
6. Performance Optimization Strategies

6.1 Algorithmic and Code-Level Optimizations
Before reaching for native extensions, developers should explore optimization opportunities within Python itself. Algorithmic improvements often yield the most dramatic speedups; an O(n log n) algorithm will outperform an O(n^2) algorithm regardless of implementation language. Python’s standard library provides optimized implementations of common algorithms and data structures: sorting with the sorted() function uses Timsort, dictionaries are implemented as highly optimized hash tables, and the heapq module provides efficient priority queue operations. Using built-in functions and standard library modules is generally faster than equivalent pure Python implementations, as the built-ins are implemented in C.
List comprehensions and generator expressions offer both readability and performance benefits over explicit loops. The comprehension syntax is compiled to specialized bytecode that avoids function call overhead for each iteration. For numerical operations, list comprehensions can be 20-30% faster than equivalent for loops with append() calls. Generator expressions provide memory efficiency by yielding values lazily, which is particularly valuable when processing large datasets or infinite sequences. The itertools module provides additional tools for efficient iteration, including functions for grouping, filtering, and combining iterables without creating intermediate lists.


6.2 Leveraging NumPy and Scientific Python
For numerical computing, NumPy represents the cornerstone of Python’s performance story. NumPy arrays provide efficient storage and operations for homogeneous numerical data, implemented as contiguous memory buffers with C-level operations. Vectorized operations in NumPy eliminate Python loop overhead by performing operations on entire arrays with single function calls. Under the hood, NumPy leverages highly optimized linear algebra libraries (BLAS and LAPACK) and can utilize SIMD instructions for parallel computation. A simple element-wise operation on a large array can be 50-100 times faster with NumPy than with pure Python loops, making NumPy essential for scientific computing and data analysis.
The NumPy ecosystem extends to libraries like SciPy for scientific algorithms, Pandas for data manipulation, and scikit-learn for machine learning. These libraries are built on NumPy’s foundation, inheriting its performance characteristics while providing domain-specific functionality. The concept of “array programming” or “vectorization” is central to achieving performance with NumPy: expressing computations as operations on entire arrays rather than element-by-element operations enables the library to dispatch to optimized C and Fortran implementations. Understanding broadcasting rules and memory layout (C-contiguous vs. Fortran-contiguous) enables further optimization for specific use cases.


6.3 Profiling and Measurement
Effective optimization requires systematic measurement. Python provides several profiling tools to identify performance bottlenecks. The cProfile module offers deterministic profiling with reasonable overhead, producing statistics on function call counts and execution times. For line-level profiling, tools like line_profiler enable identification of slow lines within functions. Memory profiling with tools like memory_profiler helps identify memory leaks and excessive allocation. The principle of “measure first, optimize second” is particularly important in Python, where intuition about performance can be misleading due to the complexity of the interpreter’s behavior.
Benchmarking requires careful methodology to produce meaningful results. Python’s timing functions (time.time(), time.perf_counter()) have different resolutions and use cases. The timeit module provides reliable micro-benchmarking by running code multiple times and measuring total elapsed time. For comparative benchmarks, controlling for JIT warmup (in implementations like PyPy), garbage collection timing, and system load is essential. Statistical analysis of benchmark results, including measures of variance and confidence intervals, helps distinguish real performance differences from measurement noise. When comparing optimization approaches, benchmarking representative workloads is crucial, as synthetic benchmarks may not reflect real-world performance characteristics.

title: Python Performance Analysis
text:
7. Comparative Performance Analysis

7.1 Python vs. Compiled Languages
Comparing Python’s performance to compiled languages reveals the fundamental trade-offs in language design. Benchmarks consistently show C and C++ executing numerical computations 10-100 times faster than equivalent Python code. The performance gap stems from multiple factors: the overhead of interpretation, dynamic type checking, Python’s object model, and the lack of compile-time optimization. A simple loop summing integers in Python might execute thousands of native instructions per iteration, while the C equivalent compiles to a handful of instructions potentially optimized further by the compiler through vectorization or loop unrolling.
However, raw execution speed tells only part of the story. Development time, code maintainability, and ecosystem productivity also factor into the total cost of software development. Python’s concise syntax, dynamic features, and extensive library ecosystem can reduce development time significantly compared to C/C++. For many applications, the development time savings outweigh the runtime cost, particularly when Python’s performance is “good enough” or when critical sections can be offloaded to optimized libraries. The rise of Python in data science and machine learning illustrates this trade-off: while the core computations may execute in C/C++/CUDA, the high-level orchestration in Python provides productivity benefits that justify its use.


7.2 Alternative Python Implementations
Several alternative Python implementations address performance through different approaches. PyPy, an implementation featuring a just-in-time compiler, can achieve 5-10x speedups on pure Python code through runtime optimization. PyPy’s JIT compiler profiles execution and generates optimized machine code for hot paths, eliminating interpretation overhead for frequently executed code. However, PyPy’s compatibility with C extensions is limited, and certain workloads may not benefit from JIT optimization. The startup overhead of JIT compilation can also impact short-running programs.
Other implementations take different approaches. Jython compiles Python to Java bytecode, enabling integration with the Java ecosystem. IronPython targets the .NET Common Language Runtime. MicroPython and CircuitPython provide Python for microcontrollers with limited resources. Each implementation makes different trade-offs between compatibility, performance, and target environment. For performance-critical applications, the choice between CPython with C extensions versus PyPy’s JIT depends on the specific workload and extension requirements. Ongoing developments in CPython itself, including the adaptive interpreter and the move toward optional GIL, may reduce the performance gap with alternative implementations.

title: Python Performance Analysis
text:
8. Conclusion

8.1 Summary of Findings
This comprehensive analysis of Python’s performance architecture reveals a language designed with deliberate trade-offs favoring developer productivity over raw execution speed. The CPython interpreter’s architecture, characterized by bytecode compilation and stack-based virtual machine execution, introduces overhead inherent to interpretation. The dynamic type system and uniform object model provide flexibility at the cost of per-operation overhead. The Global Interpreter Lock simplifies memory management and C extension integration but limits multi-threaded parallelism for CPU-bound workloads. Reference counting with generational garbage collection offers deterministic memory reclamation with some limitations.
The analysis demonstrates that Python’s performance characteristics are not simply limitations to be worked around, but consequences of design decisions that prioritize ease of use, code readability, and rapid development. Understanding these trade-offs enables informed decision-making about when Python is appropriate and how to optimize when necessary. The rich ecosystem of C extensions, from NumPy to custom native modules, provides paths to high performance when required without sacrificing Python’s productivity benefits for the majority of code.


8.2 Future Outlook
Python’s performance landscape continues to evolve. The acceptance of PEP 703 and the development of a free-threaded Python build promise to remove the GIL limitation that has constrained multi-threaded performance for decades. Ongoing work on the adaptive interpreter and potential future JIT compilation in CPython may narrow the gap with alternative implementations. The growth of Python in performance-sensitive domains like machine learning drives continued investment in optimization, benefiting the entire ecosystem. For practitioners, the key insights from this analysis inform effective Python development: leverage optimized libraries, profile before optimizing, consider C extensions for critical paths, and understand the architectural factors that influence performance to make informed design decisions.

title: The CMake Language
text:
CMake occupies an odd position. It is the de facto build system for C and C++, it is what nearly every vendor SDK ships, and it is widely disliked by the people who use it every day. All three of those are true at once, and the reason is worth understanding before you write a line of it.
CMake solves a real problem that Make does not. A makefile describes how to build a project on the machine that wrote it. Move it to a different compiler, a different operating system, or a different build tool and it needs editing. CMake describes a project’s structure abstractly and then generates the actual build files for whatever toolchain is present: Makefiles on Unix, Ninja anywhere, Visual Studio solutions on Windows, Xcode projects on macOS. One description, many builds.
The dislike is mostly about the language. CMake’s syntax accumulated over twenty-five years, everything in it is a string, and the ecosystem is layered with a decade of superseded advice that still turns up first in search results. This chapter tries to teach the current style directly, so you can skip the archaeology.






NoteRead the Make chapter first, if you have not



This chapter assumes you understand dependency graphs, targets, and incremental rebuilds as Make presents them, and it anchors nearly every concept to its Make counterpart. The complementary section Make and CMake approaches the same boundary from the other side, explaining what generates the makefiles you find in a build/ directory. There is deliberate overlap of roughly one idea, the generator model, and no more.




This is the correction that has to come first, because almost every early confusion traces to it.
CMake does not compile anything. It is a generator: it reads your project description and writes build files for some other tool to execute. Running cmake produces makefiles; running make (or ninja) builds your code. Two programs, two phases, two distinct moments at which things can go wrong.
cmake -S . -B build      # CONFIGURE: read CMakeLists.txt, write build files into build/
cmake --build build      # BUILD: invoke the generated makefiles (or ninja, or msbuild)
The second command is a portable wrapper. On a Makefiles generator it runs make -C build; you can run that yourself and it is identical. The wrapper exists so a script works unchanged when someone configures with a different generator.





flowchart LR
    A["CMakeLists.txt<br/><i>you write this</i>"] -->|"cmake -S . -B build<br/><b>configure</b>"| B["build/<br/>Makefiles or build.ninja<br/><i>generated, never edited</i>"]
    B -->|"cmake --build build<br/><b>build</b>"| C["app, libutil.a<br/><i>artifacts</i>"]
    A -.->|"edited?"| B






The dotted line matters: the generated build files list your CMakeLists.txt as a dependency, so editing one causes the next build to re-run the configure step automatically. You do not normally invoke cmake twice by hand.



If you have read Two-Phase Evaluation in the Make chapter, the shape will be familiar, and the parallel is worth drawing because it explains what CMake can and cannot know.









Phase
When
What happens
What it can see




Configure
cmake -S . -B build
CMakeLists.txt is executed top to bottom as a script. Compilers are probed, find_package searches the system, variables are set, targets are declared.
The machine, the filesystem, the toolchain


Generate
end of the same command
The accumulated target graph is written out as build files.
Everything configure produced


Build
cmake --build build
The generated build tool runs compilers and linkers.
Nothing from CMake’s variables



The crucial consequence is the same one Make has: CMake variables do not exist at build time. By the time your compiler runs, every ${VAR} has already been resolved to text and baked into the generated files. A variable you set cannot depend on something a compile step produced, for exactly the reason a Make $(shell) cannot.
CMake’s escape hatch for genuinely build-time values is the generator expression, written $<...>, which is left unresolved through configure and evaluated when the build files are written per-configuration. They look cryptic and are covered in Generator Expressions.



CMake was not designed in the abstract. It came out of a specific frustration, held by a specific person, about a specific kind of project, and nearly every one of its design decisions is traceable to that origin.
The person is Bill Hoffman. He spent the decade from 1990 to 1999 at GE’s Corporate Research Center writing large C++ systems, which meant a decade of autotools and hand-written makefiles. That is the relevant qualification: he arrived at Kitware in 1999 having already formed strong opinions about what a build system should not do, and those opinions became CMake’s design rules.
Kitware itself had been founded the year before by five people leaving GE, and it existed to support the Visualization Toolkit (VTK), a large C++ library for 3D graphics. VTK had a problem CMake would later be built to solve: it was C++ source shipped to research labs running every Unix variant of the era, plus Windows, and every one of those labs had to compile it themselves.


Two homegrown tools preceded CMake, and both are instructive failures.
pcmaker was written by Ken Martin, another Kitware founder, to get VTK building on Windows. It was a C program that read Unix makefiles and translated them into NMake files, NMake being Microsoft’s makefile tool. Your instinct to go looking for it was right and the trail is not quite cold: pcmaker lives on in VTK’s repository history at Kitware, where pcmaker/pcmaker.dsp carries commits by Ken Martin dating to November 1998. The .dsp extension dates it precisely, since that is a Visual Studio 6 project file, meaning the tool that generated Windows builds needed a hand-maintained Windows project of its own to build itself. It was never a released product, which is why there is nothing to find outside VTK’s history: it was internal scaffolding for one library’s Windows port.
gmake, in this context, is not GNU Make but Kitware’s own tool of the same name, which supported Unix and Windows compilers together. It worked, and its design had problems its authors found hard to fix.
Both tools proved the concept and shared one flaw that turned out to be fatal:






ImportantThe flaw that produced CMake



Both pcmaker and gmake required Windows developers to build from the command line. That was a reasonable expectation on Unix and an unreasonable one on Windows, where the overwhelming majority of C++ developers worked inside Visual Studio and expected a project file they could open. A cross-platform build tool that ignores how half its users actually work is not cross-platform. This is the origin of CMake’s generator model: not an architectural flourish, but a concession that the native build tool on each platform is the one that must run.





In 1999 the National Library of Medicine put Kitware on a team of three companies and three universities to build an open-source C++ toolkit for segmenting and registering medical images: the Insight Toolkit (ITK), part of the Visible Human Project. Kitware won the slot on VTK’s reputation.
The contract was unusually permissive about implementation and specific about one thing: the toolkit had to be portable to Unix, Windows, and Mac. Hoffman blended ideas from pcmaker with the parts of autotools he thought worth keeping, and CMake was first implemented in 2000.
Four rules came out of that period, and they still explain the tool:







Rule
Consequence you meet today




Support native build tools, including the Visual Studio IDE
The generator model: CMake writes build files, it does not build


One input file for every platform
CMakeLists.txt describes structure, never commands


Depend on nothing but a C++ compiler
The hand-written language, and no runtime to install


Be able to generate code, for language wrapping
configure_file(), and CMake’s use as a scripting tool






The third rule is the one that produced CMake’s most criticized feature, and it deserves stating in full because the tradeoff was made deliberately and with open eyes.

Tcl (Tool Command Language) is a high-level, general-purpose, interpreted, dynamic programming language. It was designed with the goal of being very simple and powerful. Tcl casts everything into the mold of a command, even programming constructs like variable assignment and procedure definition. Tcl supports multiple programming paradigms, including object-oriented, imperative, functional, and procedural styles.

Tcl was the obvious choice. It was the embeddable scripting language of the late 1990s, Kitware knew it well (VTK was scriptable in Tcl), and adopting it would have spared everyone the language you are about to learn. They declined, for a reason that sounds mundane and is not: a build system is the most basic dependency a package has, and it cannot itself be hard to install.
If CMake required Tcl, then building any CMake project would first require building Tcl, which in 1999 was genuinely painful on Windows and on several commercial Unixes. That is a circular dependency at exactly the worst point in the chain. So CMake depends on a C++ compiler and nothing else, which is a safe assumption when the thing it is building is C++.
Hoffman has been candid that the cost was real. Writing in The Architecture of Open Source Applications, he notes that the decision “did limit CMake to creating its own simple language, a choice that still causes some people to dislike CMake,” and adds the counterfactual that matters: had CMake been Tcl-based, “it is unlikely it would have gained the popularity it enjoys today.”
That is the trade in one sentence. The language is worse than Tcl. The tool spread because it asked nothing of you but a compiler, and Tcl-based competitors did not spread at all. Every complaint about CMake’s syntax is a bill for a decision that is the reason you have heard of CMake.






NoteThe constraint has not expired



It is tempting to read this as a 1999 problem solved by 2026. It is not. Air-gapped machines, hardened build environments, and supercomputer login nodes all still make “just install this other runtime first” an expensive request. A build system that bootstraps from a compiler alone remains genuinely valuable in exactly the environments where builds matter most.





ITK shipped, VTK moved onto CMake, and ParaView followed. That brought in the national laboratories (Los Alamos, Sandia, Livermore) as collaborators and funders, which is how a build system for one medical imaging toolkit became infrastructure.
The turning point outside Kitware’s own orbit was KDE in 2006. Alexander Neundorf championed a switch away from the scons build then in use; Kitware prototyped a KDE build in a few weeks, and it built more of KDE than scons managed. A desktop environment of that size adopting CMake is what moved it from “the toolkit build system” to a default. LLVM followed in 2016, Visual Studio added native CMake support in 2017, and Qt adopted it in 2019.







Year
Event




1998
Kitware founded; Ken Martin writes pcmaker to build VTK on Windows


1999
Bill Hoffman joins from GE Research; NLM funds ITK, requiring Unix, Windows, and Mac


2000
CMake first implemented


2003
Mastering CMake published, by Ken Martin and Bill Hoffman


2006
KDE migrates from scons; the first large adopter outside Kitware’s projects


2014
CMake 3.0: the target-based commands arrive, and “Modern CMake” begins


2016 onward
LLVM (2016), Visual Studio integration (2017), Qt (2019)



That 2014 row is the one with practical consequences for reading other people’s projects. CMake 3.0 introduced the target-based model this chapter teaches, and it split the ecosystem’s advice in two. Everything written before it, which is a great deal of what search engines still return first, teaches the directory-scoped commands: include_directories(), add_definitions(), link_libraries(). Those still work, they are still everywhere, and they are the style this chapter tells you not to use. When a tutorial’s CMake looks nothing like what you read here, check its date first.

title: The CMake Language
text:
CMake in 2 Minutes

Everything you need to be productive, before the details arrive

The rest of this chapter is thorough. This section is not: it is the smallest set of things that lets you read a CMakeLists.txt, change it correctly, and build it. If you are already working in a CMake project and want the ground under your feet before the theory, start here and treat everything after it as reference.

The Two Commands
cmake -S . -B build          # configure: read CMakeLists.txt, generate build/
cmake --build build          # build: actually compile
Run the first once. Run the second whenever you change code. If you change CMakeLists.txt, the second one re-runs the first for you.
When something is inexplicably wrong, delete and start over. This is cheap, safe, and the standard first move:
rm -rf build && cmake -S . -B build


A Whole Project
This is a complete, working CMake project. Not a fragment, not a simplification:
cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.16)
project(demo LANGUAGES C)

add_executable(app main.c util.c)
Three lines. A version floor, a project name, and a target built from two sources. Everything else in this chapter is refinement of that shape.


The Five Commands That Matter
Ninety percent of real CMakeLists.txt content is these:








Command
What it does
Make equivalent




add_executable(app a.c b.c)
Declare a program
A rule producing a binary


add_library(util a.c b.c)
Declare a library
A rule producing .a by default


target_link_libraries(app PRIVATE util)
app depends on util
-lutil, plus the dependency edge


target_include_directories(util PUBLIC inc)
Header search path
-Iinc in CFLAGS


target_compile_definitions(app PRIVATE FAST=1)
Preprocessor define
-DFAST=1 in CFLAGS



Notice the shape they share. Every one names a target first and applies something to it. That is the entire model: you are not writing build commands, you are attaching properties to named things.
That “by default” is doing real work. add_library() takes an optional type keyword, and leaving it out is a deliberate choice rather than a shorthand:
add_library(util STATIC a.c b.c)   # always static:  libutil.a
add_library(util SHARED a.c b.c)   # always shared:  libutil.so, .dylib, or .dll
add_library(util a.c b.c)          # let the person building decide
With no keyword, the BUILD_SHARED_LIBS variable decides, and it defaults to off. So the same three-line file produces libutil.a normally and libutil.dylib when configured with -DBUILD_SHARED_LIBS=ON, with nothing edited in between. The extension follows the platform too: .so on Linux, .dylib on macOS, .dll on Windows. You never name any of them, which is the “describe structure, not commands” principle from the overview showing up in a small way.
The convention is worth knowing when reading other people’s projects. Omitting the keyword leaves the linkage decision to whoever builds your library, which is the polite default for something others consume; naming STATIC or SHARED explicitly takes that decision away from them, which is right when your project genuinely requires one.


Adding a File
The single most common edit. Find the target and add the filename:
add_executable(app main.c util.c parser.c)    # parser.c is new
That is genuinely it. There is no dependency to declare, no header to list, no rule to write. CMake finds the headers parser.c includes and rebuilds it when they change, which is the hand-rolled -MMD machinery from the Make chapter, done for you.
If your project instead has a set(SOURCES ...) list feeding add_executable(app ${SOURCES}), add it there. Same idea, one more level of indirection.


PRIVATE or PUBLIC?
The one decision in routine list management that is not mechanical. The question to ask is always the same:
Does anything that links this target also need this setting?

No → PRIVATE. It is an implementation detail.
Yes → PUBLIC. It travels to consumers.

Concretely: if util.h is a header your library’s users include, then the directory containing it is PUBLIC. If a define only affects how util.c compiles internally, it is PRIVATE. When you are linking a library into an executable, PRIVATE is nearly always right, because nothing links an executable.
Get this wrong in the PUBLIC-should-have-been direction and the symptom is distinctive: your library builds fine, and the program using it fails with “no such file” on your header.


Four Things That Will Bite You
Set a build type. Without it you get no optimization flags at all:
cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
Do not edit anything in build/. It is generated output. The next configure overwrites it.
if(hello) is false. Only ON, YES, TRUE, Y, and non-zero numbers are true. A non-empty string is not truthy the way it is in Python or C.
Quoting a list destroys it. set(SOURCES a.c b.c) is three files; set(SOURCES "a.c b.c") is one filename with a space in it.


Reading a Project You Did Not Write
Two commands answer most questions:
cmake --build build --verbose        # show the real compiler invocations
cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_EXPORT_COMPILE_COMMANDS=ON
# then read build/compile_commands.json for the exact flags per file
The second is the one to reach for when a file is being compiled with flags you cannot account for. It is also what clangd and most editor tooling read, so turning it on is worth doing permanently.






TipVendor SDKs will not look like this



If you are working in an embedded project built on a vendor SDK (the Raspberry Pi Pico SDK, ESP-IDF, STM32Cube), its CMakeLists.txt will contain commands found in no CMake documentation: pico_sdk_init(), pico_add_extra_outputs(), and the like. These are functions the SDK defines, layered on top of the model above. The five commands in this section still do what this section says; the SDK’s own commands wrap large amounts of target configuration you would otherwise write by hand. When SDK code looks unfamiliar, it is the SDK, not a gap in the fundamentals.

title: The CMake Language
text:
The Language

Everything is a string, and it explains almost every surprise

CMake’s syntax is uniform to the point of monotony: the entire language is commands with arguments.
command_name(argument1 argument2 argument3)
There are no operators, no expressions, no infix arithmetic. set(), if(), add_executable(), and target_link_libraries() are all the same kind of thing. Command names are case-insensitive by convention written lowercase; variable names are case-sensitive and conventionally uppercase.
Comments start with #. Arguments are separated by whitespace, and there are no commas, which is the first thing to unlearn from every other language.

Variables and the String-Typed Truth
set() defines a variable, ${NAME} expands it:
set(PROJECT_AUTHOR "Curtis")
message(STATUS "author is ${PROJECT_AUTHOR}")
Now the fact that governs everything else: CMake has exactly one data type, the string. A list is a string with semicolons in it.
set(SOURCES a.c b.c c.c)
message(STATUS "${SOURCES}")     # prints: a.c;b.c;c.c
Those semicolons are not display formatting. They are literally the value. set() with multiple arguments joins them with semicolons, and every command that “takes a list” is really receiving one string and splitting it again.
This is why quoting changes meaning so drastically:
set(SOURCES a.c b.c c.c)         # a list of three
set(QUOTED "a.c b.c c.c")        # ONE string containing spaces
list(LENGTH SOURCES n) gives 3; the same on QUOTED gives 1. Passing QUOTED to add_executable() asks for a single file with spaces in its name, which does not exist, and the error will be about a missing source file rather than about quoting.






WarningUnset variables expand to nothing, silently



${TYPO} where TYPO was never defined expands to the empty string with no warning. A misspelled variable does not fail; it quietly vanishes, and the resulting build is subtly wrong. This is the same hazard as Make’s undefined-variable expansion, and it has the same remedy: configure with --warn-uninitialized when hunting one down, and be disciplined about names.



Variable Scope
Variables are scoped to the directory and inherited downward. A set() in the top-level CMakeLists.txt is visible in every add_subdirectory() beneath it; a set() in a subdirectory is not visible to its parent or its siblings. Functions introduce their own scope; macros do not.
set(VAR value PARENT_SCOPE) writes into the enclosing scope, and it is the usual way a subdirectory or function returns a value. Note that it sets the variable in the parent only, leaving the local one untouched, which reads as a bug the first time you meet it.
This directory-based scoping is the strongest reason to prefer target properties over variables. A variable’s reach depends on where it was written; a target property travels with the target.



if() and Its Peculiar Rules
if() is where CMake’s string-typedness produces genuine surprises, and it is worth two minutes now to save an afternoon later.
Bare words are auto-dereferenced. In an if(), an unquoted argument that names a variable is replaced by that variable’s value:
set(FOO BAR)
set(BAR "surprise")

if(FOO STREQUAL "BAR")     # TRUE: FOO's value is the string "BAR"
Read that twice. FOO was compared as its value, not its name. This behavior is unique to if() and exists for backward compatibility with CMake 1.x, and it is why you will see defensive quoting like if("${FOO}" STREQUAL "BAR") in careful code.
Truthiness is a fixed list, not a general notion. Only these are true:







True
False




ON, YES, TRUE, Y
OFF, NO, FALSE, N


Any non-zero number (1, 42, -1)
0, the empty string



NOTFOUND, anything ending in -NOTFOUND, IGNORE



Any other string, including hello



That last row catches people from every other language: if(hello) is false, because hello is not in the true list. A non-empty string is not truthy in CMake.
The -NOTFOUND suffix rule is deliberate design rather than an oddity. find_library() sets its output variable to SOMELIB-NOTFOUND on failure, so if(SOMELIB) reads naturally and the failed value carries a diagnostic name into any error message that prints it.
Comparison operators are words. There is no ==, <, or &&:
if(A STREQUAL B)              # string equality
if(N GREATER 5)               # numeric
if(VER VERSION_LESS 3.20)     # version-aware: 3.9 < 3.20
if(NOT A AND B OR C)          # boolean operators are words too
if(DEFINED SOMEVAR)           # is it set at all
if(TARGET util)               # does this target exist
if(EXISTS ${path})            # filesystem check
VERSION_LESS earns its own mention: it compares dotted versions component-wise, so 3.9 VERSION_LESS 3.20 is true where STRLESS would say the opposite.


Control Flow and Functions
Loops and conditionals close with a matching keyword, and older CMake required repeating the condition inside it (endif(SOMETHING)), which you will see in old projects. Do not imitate it; the bare form is correct and has been for years.
foreach(src IN LISTS SOURCES)
    message(STATUS "source: ${src}")
endforeach()

foreach(i RANGE 1 5)
    message(STATUS "i = ${i}")
endforeach()

while(CONDITION)
    # ...
endwhile()
The IN LISTS form is the one to use. Plain foreach(src ${SOURCES}) works by accident of expansion and breaks on empty elements.
Functions and macros both exist, and the difference matters:
function(add_demo name)
    add_executable(${name} ${name}.c)
    target_link_libraries(${name} PRIVATE util)
endfunction()

add_demo(demo1)
add_demo(demo2)
Arguments arrive as ${ARGV0}, ${ARGV1}, and so on, with ${ARGN} holding everything past the named parameters. A function has its own variable scope, so set() inside it is local unless you say PARENT_SCOPE. A macro is textual substitution with no scope of its own, which means it can clobber the caller’s variables. Prefer function() unless you specifically need to modify the caller’s scope.

title: The CMake Language
section: Targets Are the Unit of Thought
text:
Targets Are the Unit of Thought

The single idea that separates modern CMake from the bad old style

Everything above is syntax. This section is the actual model, and internalizing it is most of what it takes to write CMake that does not hurt.
In Make, a target is a filename in a dependency graph, and build settings are global strings (CFLAGS, LDFLAGS) that every rule shares. In CMake, a target is an object with properties, and those properties propagate along the dependency graph. That difference is the whole reason large projects migrated.

Declaring Targets
Three commands create targets:
add_executable(app main.c)                  # a program
add_library(util STATIC util.c)             # a static library (.a)
add_library(shared SHARED shared.c)         # a shared library (.so / .dylib / .dll)
add_library(headers INTERFACE)              # header-only: no sources to compile
Omitting STATIC/SHARED lets the BUILD_SHARED_LIBS variable decide, which is the polite default for a library others may consume.
Note that CMake needs no equivalent of a pattern rule, and no -MMD dependency generation. It knows the sources because you listed them, and header dependencies are discovered automatically by the generated build files. The hand-rolled dependency machinery that a serious makefile requires simply is not a topic here.


Properties and the Propagation Keywords
Settings attach to targets with the target_* family. Each takes one of three keywords that decide who inherits the setting:









Keyword
Applies to the target
Applies to consumers
Use for




PRIVATE
yes
no
Implementation details


PUBLIC
yes
yes
Anything the header exposes


INTERFACE
no
yes
Header-only libraries



The commands themselves map cleanly onto their Make counterparts:



Make
CMake




-I paths in CFLAGS
target_include_directories()


-D defines in CFLAGS
target_compile_definitions()


Other CFLAGS
target_compile_options()


-l and LDFLAGS
target_link_libraries()


-std=c11
target_compile_features()





Propagation, Demonstrated
Here is the mechanism doing its work, because it is easier to believe from output than from description. A library declares one PUBLIC and one PRIVATE setting:
# lib/CMakeLists.txt
add_library(util util.c)
target_include_directories(util PUBLIC ${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR})
target_compile_definitions(util
    PUBLIC  UTIL_PUBLIC=1
    PRIVATE UTIL_PRIVATE=1)
# src/CMakeLists.txt
add_executable(app main.c)
target_link_libraries(app PRIVATE util)
Configuring with -DCMAKE_EXPORT_COMPILE_COMMANDS=ON and reading the resulting compile_commands.json shows exactly what each file was compiled with:
util.c     ['-DUTIL_PRIVATE=1', '-DUTIL_PUBLIC=1', '-I/tmp/demo/lib']
main.c     ['-DUTIL_PUBLIC=1', '-I/tmp/demo/lib']
Three things to notice. main.c picked up -I/tmp/demo/lib even though src/CMakeLists.txt never mentions that path; the dependency carried its own include requirement along the link edge. It picked up UTIL_PUBLIC for the same reason. And it did not pick up UTIL_PRIVATE, because that was declared an implementation detail.
In Make, the equivalent is a global CFLAGS containing every include path in the project, edited by hand, applied to every file whether it needs them or not, with no way to express “this path is my business, not yours.” That is the improvement, stated concretely.






ImportantThe single most valuable rule in CMake



Use target_* commands, never the directory-scoped ones. The older include_directories(), add_definitions(), and link_libraries() apply to everything in the current directory and below, silently, regardless of whether it makes sense. They are the CMake equivalent of a global variable, they are what most pre-2015 tutorials teach, and they are the root of a large fraction of unmaintainable CMake. If you are reading a project full of them, you are reading the old style.




Linking Is Dependency Declaration
target_link_libraries() is badly named. It does not only pass -l flags; it declares a dependency edge, and everything propagates along it:
target_link_libraries(app PRIVATE util)
This one line says: build util before app, link it in, and apply all of util’s PUBLIC and INTERFACE properties to app. Include paths, definitions, compile options, and language standards all travel this edge. It is closer to import than to a linker flag.
The keyword here answers a different question than it does elsewhere: does anything linking app also need util? For an executable, nothing links it, so PRIVATE is nearly always right. For a library whose headers expose types from another library, PUBLIC is required, or your consumers will fail to compile.

title: The CMake Language
text:
A Complete Project

The chapter’s running example, entire

Everything so far, assembled into a project that builds a library and a program that uses it.
demo/
├── CMakeLists.txt
├── lib/
│   ├── CMakeLists.txt
│   ├── util.c
│   └── util.h
└── src/
    ├── CMakeLists.txt
    └── main.c
# CMakeLists.txt  (top level)
cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.16)
project(demo VERSION 1.0 LANGUAGES C)

set(CMAKE_C_STANDARD 11)
set(CMAKE_C_STANDARD_REQUIRED ON)
set(CMAKE_EXPORT_COMPILE_COMMANDS ON)

add_subdirectory(lib)
add_subdirectory(src)
# lib/CMakeLists.txt
add_library(util util.c)
target_include_directories(util PUBLIC ${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR})
target_compile_options(util PRIVATE -Wall -Wextra)
# src/CMakeLists.txt
add_executable(app main.c)
target_link_libraries(app PRIVATE util)
target_compile_options(app PRIVATE -Wall -Wextra)
Building it:
cmake -S . -B build          # configure
cmake --build build          # build
./build/src/app              # run
Three commands worth knowing about the first line. -S names the source directory, -B the build directory, and the fact that they are separate is not incidental: out-of-source builds are the norm in CMake, unlike Make where in-tree builds are the default. Everything generated lands in build/, nothing pollutes your source tree, and rm -rf build is a complete and safe clean.
cmake_minimum_required() must be the first command in the top-level file. It does more than check a version; it sets policy defaults, CMake’s mechanism for changing behavior without breaking old projects. Declaring 3.16 means you get 3.16-era semantics even on CMake 4.x.






Noteproject() is not decoration



project() triggers compiler detection, which is why it must appear before any target. It also defines a family of variables (demo_VERSION, PROJECT_SOURCE_DIR, CMAKE_PROJECT_NAME) that the rest of the file and any tooling can read. Omitting it produces confusing failures about the compiler being unset.



Adding Options
Real projects need switches. option() declares a cached boolean the user can flip from the command line:
option(DEMO_BUILD_TESTS "Build the test suite" ON)
option(DEMO_USE_DOUBLE  "Use double precision" OFF)

if(DEMO_USE_DOUBLE)
    target_compile_definitions(util PUBLIC DEMO_DOUBLE=1)
endif()
cmake -S . -B build -DDEMO_BUILD_TESTS=OFF -DDEMO_USE_DOUBLE=ON
Prefixing option names with the project name is a convention worth following, because options are global and a project used as a subdirectory of another can otherwise collide with its parent.


The Cache
option() writes into the cache, and understanding it prevents a category of baffling behavior.
build/CMakeCache.txt is a plain text file holding every option, detected compiler path, and found library location from the configure step. It persists between runs, which is why the second cmake -S . -B build is fast and why it remembers settings you passed only once.
It is also why changing a setting sometimes appears not to work. A cached variable is not overwritten by set() in your CMakeLists.txt unless you pass FORCE, by design: your file should not silently override what the user asked for. When a configure result seems stuck, the reliable fix is to delete build/ and start over. This is cheap, safe, and the standard advice.
rm -rf build && cmake -S . -B build      # the CMake equivalent of `make clean`

title: The CMake Language
text:
Using Other People’s Code

The problem CMake exists to solve

Nothing above justifies CMake over a competent makefile. This section does. Finding and consuming dependencies portably is where hand-written Make becomes genuinely painful and CMake earns its place.

find_package()
The standard mechanism asks the system for a dependency:
find_package(Threads REQUIRED)
target_link_libraries(app PRIVATE Threads::Threads)
REQUIRED makes a failure fatal at configure time, with a clear message, rather than a mysterious linker error much later. Without it, you check if(Threads_FOUND) and adapt.
The Threads::Threads spelling is an imported target, and the double colon is a useful signal: it means “this is a target, not a filename,” and CMake will error immediately if no such target exists rather than passing an unrecognized string to the linker. Modern packages provide imported targets that carry their own include paths and flags, so linking one is all you need.


FetchContent
When a dependency is not installed, FetchContent downloads and builds it as part of your project:
include(FetchContent)

FetchContent_Declare(fmt
    GIT_REPOSITORY https://github.com/fmtlib/fmt.git
    GIT_TAG        10.2.1)              # pin a tag, never a branch

FetchContent_MakeAvailable(fmt)

target_link_libraries(app PRIVATE fmt::fmt)
This is the closest CMake comes to Cargo or pip, and the comparison is instructive about how much less it does. There is no lockfile, no transitive version resolution, and no central registry. Two dependencies wanting different versions of a third is a problem you solve by hand. Pinning GIT_TAG to an exact tag or commit is not optional advice; a branch name makes your build non-reproducible.






NoteWhy C++ dependency management is like this



C and C++ never had a package manager in the language’s first four decades, so the ecosystem grew around system packages and vendored source trees. CMake inherited that world rather than creating it. vcpkg and Conan are the serious attempts at the missing layer, both integrate with CMake, and neither has become universal. If Rust’s Cargo felt like an unreasonable luxury, this is the contrast that explains why.

title: The CMake Language
text:
Generator Expressions

The $<...> syntax, and when you actually need it

Generator expressions are the feature most likely to make CMake look unreadable, and they exist for a precise reason: some values are not known at configure time because they depend on which build configuration is being generated.
A single configure can produce build files for Debug and Release simultaneously (Visual Studio and Xcode do this by default). A if(CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE STREQUAL "Debug") cannot work there, because configure runs once for all configurations. $<...> defers the decision:
target_compile_options(app PRIVATE
    $<$<CONFIG:Debug>:-O0 -g>
    $<$<CONFIG:Release>:-O2 -DNDEBUG>)
The form is $<condition:value>: emit value only if condition holds. The commonest ones:



Expression
Meaning




$<CONFIG:Debug>
1 in the Debug configuration


$<CXX_COMPILER_ID:GNU>
1 when compiling with GCC


$<PLATFORM_ID:Windows>
1 on Windows


$<TARGET_FILE:app>
Full path to a target’s output file


$<BUILD_INTERFACE:...>
Applies when built in-tree


$<INSTALL_INTERFACE:...>
Applies when consumed after install



The last two solve a specific problem worth naming: a library’s include directory differs depending on whether a consumer builds it as a subdirectory or links it after installation. The idiom is:
target_include_directories(util PUBLIC
    $<BUILD_INTERFACE:${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}/include>
    $<INSTALL_INTERFACE:include>)
Do not reach for generator expressions early. Most projects need only the CONFIG: form for per-configuration flags, and reading a $<...> correctly is easier than deciding you need one.

title: The CMake Language
text:
Build Types and Toolchains

Build Types
CMake ships four standard configurations, selected with CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE on single-configuration generators (Makefiles, Ninja):








Type
Flags (GCC/Clang defaults)
Purpose




Debug
-g
Debugging: no optimization, full symbols


Release
-O3 -DNDEBUG
Shipping


RelWithDebInfo
-O2 -g -DNDEBUG
Profiling, and debugging optimized code


MinSizeRel
-Os -DNDEBUG
Size-constrained targets



cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
The trap: if you do not set it, it is empty, and you get no optimization flags at all. Not -O0, but nothing, which is usually -O0 by compiler default. A great many “CMake builds are slow” complaints are an unset build type. Since separate build directories are cheap, keeping build-debug/ and build-release/ side by side is the common practice, and it neatly avoids the stale-object problem that variant builds cause in Make.


Cross-Compilation
For the embedded work in the C and Assembly chapters, cross-compiling is the main event, and CMake handles it with a toolchain file: a small script that describes the target system, read before anything else.
# arm-none-eabi.cmake
set(CMAKE_SYSTEM_NAME      Generic)        # "Generic" means bare metal, no OS
set(CMAKE_SYSTEM_PROCESSOR arm)

set(CMAKE_C_COMPILER   arm-none-eabi-gcc)
set(CMAKE_CXX_COMPILER arm-none-eabi-g++)

# the compiler cannot link a host test program, so relax the check
set(CMAKE_TRY_COMPILE_TARGET_TYPE STATIC_LIBRARY)

set(CMAKE_FIND_ROOT_PATH_MODE_PROGRAM NEVER)   # find host programs on the host
set(CMAKE_FIND_ROOT_PATH_MODE_LIBRARY ONLY)    # find libraries only in the sysroot
set(CMAKE_FIND_ROOT_PATH_MODE_INCLUDE ONLY)
cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_TOOLCHAIN_FILE=arm-none-eabi.cmake
Setting CMAKE_SYSTEM_NAME is what puts CMake into cross-compiling mode and sets CMAKE_CROSSCOMPILING. The TRY_COMPILE_TARGET_TYPE line addresses a specific early failure: CMake normally validates a compiler by building and linking a small program, which cannot link on a bare-metal target with no startup code or linker script, so you tell it to stop at the static library stage.
The same toolchain file is discussed from the C++ side in Cross-Compilation and Bare Metal.

title: The CMake Language
text:
Debugging CMake
The toolkit, roughly in the order you will need it.
Print a variable. The message() command with STATUS is the $(info) of CMake:
message(STATUS "SOURCES = ${SOURCES}")
message(WARNING "this is suspicious")
message(FATAL_ERROR "stop here")
See the actual compiler command. The default build output shows progress, not invocations:
cmake --build build --verbose        # or: make -C build VERBOSE=1
Generate a compile database. -DCMAKE_EXPORT_COMPILE_COMMANDS=ON writes build/compile_commands.json with the exact command for every source file. This is the fastest way to answer “what flags is this file really getting,” and it is what clangd and most editor tooling consume. Turning it on unconditionally in your top-level file is a kindness to everyone using the project.
Trace execution. --trace-expand prints every command as it runs with variables expanded. It is extremely verbose and occasionally the only thing that works:
cmake -S . -B build --trace-expand 2>&1 | less
Inspect the cache. cmake -LAH build lists every cached variable with its help text. ccmake build is a curses interface for the same thing.
Print target properties. When propagation is not doing what you expect:
get_target_property(dirs app INCLUDE_DIRECTORIES)
message(STATUS "app include dirs: ${dirs}")

title: The CMake Language
text:
Common Pitfalls
Each of these is a symptom you will actually see, with its cause.
file(GLOB) for sources. It works, and it is the wrong tool:
file(GLOB SOURCES "src/*.c")     # do not do this
The glob runs at configure time. Add a new source file and the build system does not know it exists, so nothing rebuilds and nothing tells you why. CMake’s own documentation advises against it. List sources explicitly; the maintenance cost is one line per file and the failure mode it prevents is genuinely confusing.
A stale cache. Changing a compiler or a cached option and seeing no effect almost always means the cache is holding the old value. rm -rf build.
Forgetting CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE. No optimization, and a “CMake is slow” conclusion.
Using directory-scoped commands. include_directories() instead of target_include_directories(). Works at first, becomes unmaintainable, and is the single clearest marker of pre-modern CMake.
Quoting a list. "${SOURCES}" collapses three files into one nonexistent filename with spaces.
Expecting if(string) to be true. It is false unless the string is in the truthy list.
Editing files in build/. They are output. The next configure overwrites them.
Missing PUBLIC on a library’s include directory. The library builds, consumers fail with “no such file” on its header, and the error points at the consumer rather than the cause.

title: The CMake Language
text:
Make or Ninja
CMake’s default generator on Unix is Unix Makefiles, but Ninja is the better choice for anything sizable:
cmake -S . -B build -G Ninja
Ninja was built for precisely this role: a build language nobody writes by hand, designed to be emitted by a generator and executed fast. It parallelizes by default without -j, and its no-op builds are dramatically quicker than Make’s on large projects, which matters because the no-op build is the one you run most. Your CMakeLists.txt does not change; only the generated output does.
The tradeoff is that Ninja must be installed, whereas make is everywhere. For a project others will build, Makefiles as the default with Ninja as an option is the diplomatic choice.

title: The CMake Language
text:
Key Differences from Make









Make
CMake




What it is
A build tool
A generator that emits build files


Unit of thought
A rule producing a file
A target with properties


Build settings
Global strings (CFLAGS)
Per-target, propagating along dependencies


Header dependencies
Hand-rolled with -MMD
Automatic


Out-of-source builds
Possible, awkward
The default


Portability
One platform per makefile
One description, many toolchains


Finding libraries
Hand-written, or pkg-config
find_package(), imported targets


Data types
Strings
Strings


Language quality
Terse, three languages in one file
Verbose, uniform, string-typed


Best at
Small projects, task running, anything non-C
Portable C and C++ projects with dependencies



The last row is the practical summary. For a handful of files, a task runner, or a language with its own build tool, a makefile is smaller and clearer. For a C or C++ project that must build on more than one machine and consume libraries it did not write, CMake does work you would otherwise do by hand and get wrong.
Neither is a good language. Make is three languages sharing a file with an evaluation order you have to reason about; CMake is one uniform language with a single data type and twenty-five years of accumulated compatibility. You use them because the problems they solve are real, and because the alternatives have not displaced them.
