Every rule and variable Make knows, including built-ins


make -p -f /dev/null
The built-in database alone, with none of your makefile


$(info ...)
Printf debugging during phase 1


$(origin VAR)
Where a value came from


$(flavor VAR)
Whether it was = or :=



-n (--just-print) is the first thing to reach for. It prints commands without executing them, so you can confirm what a build would do before letting it. It is also the safe way to inspect a clean or install target you did not write.
make -n install
Note one limitation: -n still expands everything, so any $(shell) call runs. A makefile that does real work at parse time is not fully inert under -n.
--trace annotates each recipe with the rule that triggered it and the reason, which is exactly the question “why is this being rebuilt.” It requires GNU Make 4.0 or newer.
--debug=b is the portable equivalent and is available on older versions including the 3.81 that macOS ships. The b is “basic”; v (verbose), i (implicit rules), and m (makefile remaking) add detail, and bare -d turns on everything at a volume that is rarely useful.
-p (--print-data-base) dumps the entire internal state: every variable with its origin, every rule including built-ins, and the files Make considered. It runs to hundreds of lines, so pipe it:
make -p | grep -A2 '^CFLAGS'
make -p -f /dev/null | less     # built-in rules with no makefile at all


A Worked Session: The Target That Always Rebuilds
This is the most common real complaint about a makefile, and it has a small number of causes. Here is a build that relinks on every invocation despite nothing changing:
CC := gcc

.PHONY: all version
all: app

app: main.o version
    $(CC) -o $@ main.o

main.o: main.c
    $(CC) -c $< -o $@

version:
    @echo "stamping version"
The symptom, on a tree where everything is already built:
$ make
stamping version
gcc -o app main.o
$ make
stamping version
gcc -o app main.o
Nothing changed, and app relinks anyway. Ask Make why:
$ make --debug=b
Updating goal targets....
 File `all' does not exist.
     File `version' does not exist.
    Must remake target `version'.
stamping version
    Successfully remade target file `version'.
   Prerequisite `version' of target `app' does not exist.
  Must remake target `app'.
gcc -o app main.o
The diagnosis is in one line: Prerequisite 'version' of target 'app' does not exist. A phony target never corresponds to a file, so it is never up to date, and anything depending on it is therefore always stale. The .PHONY declaration is correct; using that target as a prerequisite of a real file is the mistake.
The fix depends on intent. If the version stamp is genuinely an input, it must produce a real file so Make can compare timestamps:
app: main.o version.txt
    $(CC) -o $@ main.o

version.txt: $(shell git rev-parse HEAD > /dev/null && echo .git/HEAD)
    git describe --always > $@
If it is just a message, it does not belong in the graph at all; move it into the recipe:
app: main.o
    @echo "stamping version"
    $(CC) -o $@ main.o

The Other Causes
When --debug=b reports something else, the phrasing points at the cause:
File 'x' does not exist for a target you believe exists usually means a path mismatch: the rule writes build/app and something depends on app, or a VPATH search found a different file than you assumed.
A prerequisite is newer for no reason is typically a directory used as a normal prerequisite rather than an order-only one, since a directory’s mtime changes whenever a file is written into it.
Everything rebuilds after a branch switch is version control not preserving mtimes, covered in When Timestamps Lie.
A rule fires that you did not write is a built-in rule. Confirm with make -p -f /dev/null and disable them.



Debugging Phase 1
Everything above inspects the build. When the problem is a variable that is empty, wrong, or mysteriously overridden, you need the read phase instead, and the tools are the diagnostic functions:
$(info CFLAGS = "$(CFLAGS)")
$(info OBJS   = $(OBJS))
$(info origin = $(origin CC))
$(info flavor = $(flavor CFLAGS))
The quotes matter. $(info CFLAGS = $(CFLAGS)) cannot distinguish an empty variable from one holding a space, and trailing whitespace in a Make variable is both invisible and load-bearing.
$(origin) is the tool for “why is this value not what my makefile says.” It returns undefined, default, environment, file, command line, override, or automatic, which maps onto the precedence table in Where Values Come From. If $(origin CC) says environment, someone’s shell profile is in your build.
Two flags complete the set. --warn-undefined-variables catches the typo that expands to nothing:
$ make --warn-undefined-variables
Makefile:8: warning: undefined variable 'CFLGAS'
And -B (--always-make) rebuilds everything unconditionally, which is useful for separating “the graph is wrong” from “the recipe is wrong.” If make -B produces a correct result and plain make does not, the recipes are fine and the dependency graph is lying.






TipA fast triage order




make -n: is it running what you expect?
make --debug=b (or --trace): why is that target considered stale?
$(info ...) on the suspect variable: is the value what you think?
$(origin VAR): if not, where did it come from?
make -p | grep VAR: the exhaustive answer, when the first four fail.

title: Makefile Language
text:
Common Pitfalls

Nine failures, and the two ideas behind all of them

Everything that goes wrong in a makefile is collected here, stated as symptom, cause, and fix. What makes the list worth reading straight through is that these are not nine unrelated quirks. Almost every one is a boundary error between the three languages or a phase confusion, and the last column of the table below says which:







Symptom
Root cause




missing separator
Three languages: spaces where a tab marks shell


Shell variable is empty
Three languages: $ consumed by Make


cd does not persist
Three languages: one shell per recipe line


Comparison fails on equal-looking text
Three languages: invisible trailing whitespace


Variable references itself
Phases: deferred expansion loops


$(wildcard) finds nothing
Phases: parse time precedes recipes


Stale target after a failure
Timestamps: mtime updated on partial output


Works serially, fails under -j
Graph: a missing edge


make clean says up to date
Graph: a target that is also a filename




missing separator
Symptom. Makefile:5: *** missing separator.  Stop.
Cause. A recipe line indented with spaces instead of a tab. Make uses the leading tab to know a line is shell rather than rule or macro, so without it, your gcc command is parsed as a makefile construct. Finding neither = nor :, Make reports the missing separator. The message names the symptom of a failed parse, not the cause.
Fix. Use a tab. Configure the editor so it cannot happen: [{Makefile,*.mk}] with indent_style = tab in .editorconfig. Full treatment in Tabs, and Why.






WarningThe same error from an indented conditional



A tab in front of ifeq makes it a recipe line, and the shell has no ifeq. That one produces ifeq: command not found rather than missing separator, but the cause is identical: leading whitespace decided which language the line was in. Conditional bodies indent with spaces.




$ Crossing the Boundary
Symptom. A shell loop does nothing, or a command receives an empty string where a variable should be.
# BROKEN: prints "found " repeatedly
list:
    for f in *.c; do echo "found $f"; done
Cause. Make expands the recipe before handing it to the shell. $f is read by Make, which finds no variable f and substitutes nothing. The shell never sees it.
Fix. $$ escapes a dollar sign so it survives into the shell:
list:
    for f in *.c; do echo "found $$f"; done
The rule is mechanical: inside a recipe, $(...) belongs to Make and $$ belongs to the shell. This applies equally to shell command substitution, $$(date), and to awk scripts needing $$1.


cd Does Not Persist
Symptom. A recipe changes directory and the next line runs somewhere else.
Cause. Each recipe line gets its own shell process. The cd affects only the shell that ran it, which exits immediately.
Fix. Join the lines into one command, or enable .ONESHELL:
install:
    cd build && cp app /usr/local/bin/
Covered in Multi-Line Recipes; the .ONESHELL tradeoffs are in Special Targets.


Trailing Whitespace
Symptom. A conditional fails against a value that looks correct.
MODE := debug
ifeq ($(MODE),debug)      # does not match if MODE has a trailing space
Cause. Trailing whitespace is part of a Make variable’s value and is invisible in an editor. It commonly arrives from a $(shell) call or a hand-edited configuration block, and $(info MODE = $(MODE)) will not reveal it.
Fix. Quote when printing, $(info "$(MODE)"), and $(strip ...) anything whose provenance you do not control. Note also that VAR := value # comment includes the space before # in the value, which is a frequent source of this.


Recursive Variable Self-Reference
Symptom. *** Recursive variable 'A' references itself (eventually).  Stop.
Cause. A = $(A) more with = stores the right side unexpanded, so every reference re-expands it forever. Make detects the loop and refuses.
Fix. Use :=, which expands the old value once and reassigns:
A := $(A) more
Or +=, which does the right thing for appending. See The Two Flavors.


$(wildcard) Sees Nothing
Symptom. A build fails on a clean tree and succeeds on the second run.
OBJS := $(wildcard build/*.o)     # empty until something has been built
Cause. $(wildcard) runs in phase 1, before any recipe. It cannot see files a recipe is about to create. Globbing an output directory is therefore always wrong.
Fix. Derive outputs from inputs, which do exist at parse time:
SRCS := $(wildcard src/*.c)
OBJS := $(patsubst src/%.c,build/%.o,$(SRCS))
The same reasoning applies to $(shell) inspecting build products, and to conditionals testing them. See What Runs When.


A Failed Recipe Leaves a Stale Target
Symptom. A build fails, you run make again, and it reports the broken target is up to date.
Cause. The shell creates the output file before the command runs. A command that fails partway leaves a truncated file with a fresh timestamp, which Make reads as current.
Fix. One line, near the top of every makefile:
.DELETE_ON_ERROR:
This is the most consequential single line in this chapter, because the failure is silent and produces wrong output rather than an error. Full discussion in .DELETE_ON_ERROR.


Works Serially, Fails Under -j
Symptom. make succeeds, make --jobs=8 fails intermittently and passes on retry.
Cause. A missing prerequisite. The graph does not connect two targets that must be ordered, and serial execution happened to visit them in a workable order. Parallelism removes that accident.
Fix. Find the true dependency and declare it. This is not a Make bug and .NOTPARALLEL is not the answer; it hides the defect while surrendering the speedup. See Parallelism Is a Correctness Test.


make clean Says Up To Date
Symptom. make: 'clean' is up to date.
Cause. A file or directory named clean exists. Make compared the target against it, found no newer prerequisites, and concluded there was nothing to do.
Fix. Declare action targets phony:
.PHONY: all clean test install docs
A docs/ directory silently disabling make docs is the version of this you are most likely to meet. See Phony Targets.






TipThe two questions



When a makefile misbehaves, almost every cause above is reached by asking two questions in order. Which language is this line? resolves tabs, $ versus $$, the per-line shell, and stray whitespace. Which phase does this run in? resolves wildcards, shell calls, conditionals, and variable flavors. What remains after both is a graph problem: a missing edge, or a target that is secretly a filename.

title: Makefile Language
text:
Make and CMake

What generates the makefiles you were never meant to read

If you have worked in a modern C++ project, you have probably met a tree with a CMakeLists.txt in nearly every directory and wondered what collects them. That question has a clean answer, but it starts with a correction.
This section answers it from Make’s side: what generates the makefiles you find in a build/ directory, and how CMake’s structure differs from recursive make. For CMake as a language in its own right, its target model, its syntax, and how to write it, see The CMake Language.






ImportantCMakeLists.txt is not a makefile



CMake is a separate language with its own syntax and semantics. It shares nothing with Make beyond a problem domain. If you read CMakeLists.txt expecting makefile constructs, nothing will parse: there are no tab-indented recipes, no $(VAR) expansions with Make’s meaning, and no target: prerequisites rules.


More importantly, CMake is not a build tool at all. It is a generator. It reads your CMakeLists.txt tree once, at configure time, and writes out real build files for some other tool to execute. By default on Unix that other tool is Make, so the thing that actually builds your project is a set of generated makefiles that no human wrote and no human should edit.
cmake -S . -B build      # configure: read CMakeLists.txt, generate build/
cmake --build build      # build: run the generated makefiles
That two-step split is the whole architecture. Everything else follows from it.

How the Tree Is Collected
The mechanism is add_subdirectory(). The top-level CMakeLists.txt names its children, each child is read in turn, and each may name children of its own:
# CMakeLists.txt (top level)
cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.16)
project(demo C)

add_subdirectory(lib)
add_subdirectory(src)
# lib/CMakeLists.txt
add_library(util util.c)
target_include_directories(util PUBLIC ${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR})
# src/CMakeLists.txt
add_executable(app main.c)
target_link_libraries(app PRIVATE util)
Reading is recursive, but the result is not. Every directory contributes its targets to one global picture, and CMake emits a single flat build graph covering the entire project.





flowchart TD
    A["CMakeLists.txt<br/>add_subdirectory(lib)<br/>add_subdirectory(src)"] --> B["lib/CMakeLists.txt<br/>add_library(util)"]
    A --> C["src/CMakeLists.txt<br/>add_executable(app)"]
    B --> D["One global build graph<br/>util → app"]
    C --> D
    D --> E["Generated makefiles<br/>in build/"]






This distinction is the one that matters, because the directory layout looks exactly like recursive make and behaves like its opposite:









Recursive Make
CMake




Per-directory file
A real makefile, executed
Input read at configure time


Resulting graph
One fragment per directory
One graph for the whole project


Cross-directory dependencies
Invisible to each sub-make
Fully known


Parallelism
Limited by the recursion structure
Across the entire project



Recursive make suffers because each sub-make sees only its own fragment. CMake reads a tree and produces a whole, which is precisely the fix Peter Miller argued for.






NoteThe generated makefiles are not recursive either



CMake does write a Makefile into each mirrored build directory, which makes it look recursive. Those are thin conveniences: each one immediately cds to the build root and delegates to a single CMakeFiles/Makefile2 holding the real graph. Running make from a subdirectory still builds against complete dependency information.




The Concept Map
Most Make concepts have a CMake counterpart, with one genuine conceptual leap at the end.







Make
CMake




A rule producing a binary
add_executable(app main.c)


A rule producing a library
add_library(util util.c)


CFLAGS
target_compile_options(), target_compile_definitions()


-I include paths
target_include_directories()


LDFLAGS, -l
target_link_libraries()


VAR = value
set(VAR value), scoped to the directory and below


Cross-compile variable block
A toolchain file, -DCMAKE_TOOLCHAIN_FILE=...


Hand-written -MMD dependency generation
Automatic



The leap is that a CMake target is an object with properties, not just a name in a graph. Those properties propagate along the link graph according to a keyword you choose:

PRIVATE: needed to build this target, not exposed to its consumers.
PUBLIC: needed to build this target and by anything that links it.
INTERFACE: not needed by this target, only by its consumers (typical for header-only libraries).

In the example above, lib/CMakeLists.txt declares its include directory PUBLIC. So when src/CMakeLists.txt says target_link_libraries(app PRIVATE util), the compile line for main.c picks up -I/path/to/lib automatically. Nothing in src/CMakeLists.txt mentions that path. The dependency carried its own build requirements along with it.
This has no equivalent in Make, where include paths are a global CFLAGS string that every rule shares and every developer edits by hand. It is the main reason large projects moved to CMake, and the main thing to internalize when reading one.


Reading a CMake Project
A few things make a generated build tractable when you need to debug it.
See the real compiler command. The default output shows progress, not invocations:
make -C build VERBOSE=1        # or: cmake --build build --verbose
Generate a compile database. Configuring with -DCMAKE_EXPORT_COMPILE_COMMANDS=ON writes build/compile_commands.json, containing the exact command for every source file. Language servers such as clangd consume this, and it is the fastest way to answer “what flags is this file actually being compiled with.”
Know where the real rules live. In a Makefiles build, the per-target rules are in build/<dir>/CMakeFiles/<target>.dir/build.make, and the flags are split out into flags.make next to it. Worth reading once, to see that the generated output is ordinary Make using the same -MD dependency mechanism described in Auto-Generated Dependencies.
You do not re-run cmake by hand. The generated makefiles depend on the CMakeLists.txt files, so editing one causes the next make to re-run CMake automatically. This is the include restart mechanism applied at project scale.
Never edit anything in build/. It is output. The next configure overwrites it, and deleting the directory entirely is a normal, safe operation.


Make or Ninja
CMake’s default generator on Unix is Unix Makefiles, but Ninja is the better choice for anything large:
cmake -S . -B build -G Ninja
Ninja was designed for exactly this role: a build language nobody writes by hand, optimized for a generator to emit and for a machine to execute quickly. It parallelizes by default, and its no-op builds are dramatically faster than Make’s on large projects, which matters because a no-op build is the one you run most. The CMakeLists.txt files do not change; only the generated output does.


CMake Documentation
Modern CMake, the best guide to target-based CMake
Ninja

title: Makefile Language
text:
Where Make Sits Today

What it still wins at, and what it has lost

Make is fifty years old, and the honest assessment is neither that it is obsolete nor that the newer tools are hype. It occupies a narrower niche than it once did, and inside that niche nothing has displaced it.

What Make Still Wins At
It is already there. No installation, no version pin, no lockfile, no daemon. A makefile in a repository works on a stranger’s machine, in a container, over SSH on a box you cannot install software on. For a small project this is worth more than any feature, because the alternative starts with a paragraph of setup instructions.
Zero configuration for small builds. Ten lines gets you a correct incremental build of a C program. The equivalent CMake project is comparable in length but requires CMake, a generator, and a build directory; the ceremony does not pay off until the project is large enough to need it.
Gluing heterogeneous tools. This is where Make is genuinely unmatched, and it follows directly from The Shell Is the Recipe Language. A pipeline that renders LaTeX, converts images with ImageMagick, generates code from a schema, builds a container, and publishes the result is not a C build, and no language-native toolchain covers it. Make does, because it never assumed anything about the work. This notebook is built that way.
Task running. The command menu described in Make as a Task Runner is a legitimate modern use, and its advantage is again ubiquity rather than quality.
One person can read the whole thing. A 60-line makefile is fully comprehensible in an afternoon, including its failure modes. That is not true of a generated Ninja file or a large CMake project, and for a small team it matters.


What Make Has Lost
Large C/C++ projects, to CMake and Ninja. Not because Make cannot express them, but because target-based CMake carries build requirements along the dependency graph and Make has only a global CFLAGS string. Add cross-platform configuration and toolchain detection, which Make has no answer for at all, and the case is decided. Ninja then beats Make on raw execution speed for the generated output.
Correctness under change, to content hashing. Every failure in When Timestamps Lie is structural. Ninja, Bazel, and Cargo hash inputs, so a restored backup, a branch switch, or a regenerated-but-identical file behaves correctly. They also track flags as inputs, which is why Make needs the separate-directory trick for debug and release builds and they do not.
Hermetic and distributed builds, to Bazel. Make’s recipes can read anything on the machine, so a build is reproducible only by convention. Bazel sandboxes each action, which is what makes remote execution and shared caching possible. At a thousand engineers that is transformative; at one it is overhead.
Language-native builds, to Cargo and Go. When a language ships a build tool that understands its module system, that tool wins by default. Nobody writes a makefile to build a Rust crate, and Cargo needs no dependency graph from you because it derives one from the source.


The Idea That Outlived the Tool
The closing observation is the one from the Overview: the reason Make’s successors all look somewhat like Make is that they inherited its model rather than replaced it.
Ninja is a dependency graph with faster execution. Bazel is a dependency graph with hermetic actions and content hashing. Cargo is a dependency graph specialized to one language’s module system. CMake is a generator of dependency graphs. Every one of them is targets, prerequisites, and staleness, with the trades adjusted.
That is why learning Make pays off beyond Make. The model transfers: once you know why a build is incremental, why an incomplete graph fails under parallelism, and why timestamps are a proxy rather than an answer, you can read any of the successors and know what questions to ask. Feldman’s afternoon in 1976 produced a tool that is now a poor choice for the job it was written for, and a model that every replacement still implements.

title: Makefile Language
text:
Further Reading


GNU Make Manual. The reference, and unusually well written for a GNU manual: readable front to back, with the two-phase evaluation model explained properly.
Robert Mecklenburg, Managing Projects with GNU Make, 3rd edition (O’Reilly, 2004). The standard book. Dated in its examples and still the best extended treatment of the language itself.
Peter Miller, Recursive Make Considered Harmful (AUUG, 1997). The paper that changed how build systems are structured. Short, and the argument is as relevant as it was then.
John Graham-Cumming, The GNU Make Standard Library. A function library for Make, and a working demonstration of how far the macro language can be pushed. His GNU Make Unleashed collects his writing on debugging makefiles.
POSIX make. The portable core, worth a look to see how much of what you use is a GNU extension.
CMake Documentation and Ninja, for the tools that generate and execute what Make used to.

title: Python
text:
Python was created by Guido van Rossum in the late 1980s and first released in 1991. Van Rossum was working at CWI in the Netherlands and wanted a language that filled the gap between shell scripting (too limited) and C (too verbose for rapid development). He named it after Monty Python, not the snake.
The motivation was philosophical as much as practical: productivity matters. A program you can write in an afternoon and read back six months later is often more valuable than a highly optimized one that takes weeks to get right. Python made a deliberate bet that developer time is usually the bottleneck, not CPU time.
That bet paid off. Python is now the dominant language for data science, machine learning, scientific computing, web backends, and automation. It runs everywhere from Raspberry Pis to GPU clusters.




Every value in Python — integers, strings, functions, classes, modules — is a first-class object with an identity, a type, and a value. There are no primitives in the C sense. This uniformity makes the language consistent and extensible, at the cost of memory overhead.



Variables have no declared type. A variable is a name bound to an object, and that binding can be rebound to any object at any time. The type lives with the object, not the variable. This eliminates boilerplate but shifts type errors from compile time to runtime.



Assignment never copies an object. It copies a reference to an object. This has profound implications for mutable data, covered in depth below.



CPython (the reference implementation) uses reference counting as its primary garbage collection strategy, augmented by a cycle collector for circular references. Memory is managed for you, but understanding how it works prevents subtle bugs.



Python’s syntax enforces structure through indentation rather than braces. The language includes exactly one obvious way to do most things, by design. This is not a limitation: it is a feature that makes code written by others readable.



The standard library is enormous. Networking, file I/O, JSON, regular expressions, HTTP, CSV, database access, unit testing: most of what you need for a typical program is already there.






NoteThe Zen of Python



Tim Peters wrote nineteen aphorisms that capture Python’s design philosophy. You can read them any time with import this.


Code
# The following is a little more involved because once `this` is loaded into
# sys.modules cache, it won't render upon import. To make sure it renders
# every time we remove it from sys's module cache.
import sys

try:
    del sys.modules["this"]
except:
    pass

import this


The Zen of Python, by Tim Peters

Beautiful is better than ugly.
Explicit is better than implicit.
Simple is better than complex.
Complex is better than complicated.
Flat is better than nested.
Sparse is better than dense.
Readability counts.
Special cases aren't special enough to break the rules.
Although practicality beats purity.
Errors should never pass silently.
Unless explicitly silenced.
In the face of ambiguity, refuse the temptation to guess.
There should be one-- and preferably only one --obvious way to do it.
Although that way may not be obvious at first unless you're Dutch.
Now is better than never.
Although never is often better than *right* now.
If the implementation is hard to explain, it's a bad idea.
If the implementation is easy to explain, it may be a good idea.
Namespaces are one honking great idea -- let's do more of those!

title: Python
section: How a Python Project Is Structured
text:
How a Python Project Is Structured









Concept
C
Rust
Python




Distributable unit
.a / .so
Crate (crates.io)
Package (PyPI)


Project manifest
Makefile
Cargo.toml
pyproject.toml


Namespace / file unit
(file, no formal system)
Module (mod)
Module (.py file)


Import
#include
use
import


Package manager
(none built in)
cargo
pip


Isolated environment
(none)
(per project by default)
virtual environment




Modules
Every .py file is a module. Its name is the filename without the extension. You import it with import:
# math_utils.py
def add(a, b):
    return a + b


# main.py
import math_utils

print(math_utils.add(2, 3))

# or import specific names directly
from math_utils import add

print(add(2, 3))


Packages
A directory containing an __init__.py file is a package: a namespace that groups related modules.
my_project/
├── main.py
└── geometry/
    ├── __init__.py       # makes geometry/ a package
    ├── shapes.py         # geometry.shapes
    └── transforms.py     # geometry.transforms
__init__.py can be empty or can run initialization code and re-export names to shape the package’s public API — the Python equivalent of pub use in Rust.


Virtual Environments
Python is installed system-wide, but dependencies differ per project. A virtual environment is an isolated Python installation for a single project:
python -m venv .venv            # create a virtual environment
source .venv/bin/activate       # activate it (macOS/Linux)
pip install requests            # install into this environment only
Dependencies are recorded in pyproject.toml or requirements.txt. Always use a virtual environment; installing packages system-wide causes conflicts across projects.

title: Python
text:
The Basics

Variables and Types
Python variables are not declarations: they are name bindings. A name comes into existence the moment you assign to it, and its type is determined by the object it is bound to:
x = 42  # x is bound to an int object
x = "hello"  # x is now bound to a str object — no error
x = [1, 2, 3]  # x is now bound to a list object
The built-in scalar types:
i = 42  # int (arbitrary precision: no overflow ever)
f = 3.14  # float (64-bit IEEE 754)
c = 2 + 3j  # complex
b = True  # bool (subclass of int: True == 1, False == 0)
s = "hello"  # str (immutable Unicode sequence)
n = None  # NoneType: the absence of a value (Python's null)
No integer overflow. Python integers are arbitrary precision — they grow as large as memory allows. This is convenient and occasionally surprising in performance-sensitive code.


Type Hints

Advisory types, not enforced types

Type annotations exist but are not enforced at runtime. The interpreter ignores them entirely. They exist for static type checkers (mypy, pyright) and as documentation. This is the opposite of Rust, where types are mandatory and compiler-checked. In Python, types are advisory — useful but optional.

Basic Annotations
Variables and function signatures are annotated with : for values and parameters and -> for return types:
name: str = "alice"
count: int = 0


def add(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    return a + b


def greet(name: str) -> None:  # None means the function returns nothing
    print(f"hello, {name}")


Container Types
Built-in containers are generic as of Python 3.9. Use lowercase directly:
def total(numbers: list[int]) -> int:
    return sum(numbers)


def lookup(data: dict[str, int], key: str) -> int:
    return data[key]


coords: tuple[float, float] = (3.0, 4.0)
unique: set[str] = {"a", "b", "c"}
Before Python 3.9 the same types came from the typing module: List[int], Dict[str, int]. You will see both styles in existing code.


Optional Values
T | None marks a value that might be absent. It is Python’s loose equivalent of Option<T> in Rust, but the runtime does not enforce it:
def find_user(user_id: int) -> str | None:
    if user_id == 1:
        return "alice"
    return None
Older code uses Optional[str] from the typing module, which means exactly the same thing. The | syntax is available from Python 3.10 onward.


Union Types
A | B means a value that can be either type:
def process(value: int | str) -> str:
    return str(value)
Older code writes Union[int, str] from typing. Same meaning.


Any
Any is the escape hatch. A value typed as Any is compatible with every other type in both directions. Use it when interfacing with untyped code or when the type is genuinely dynamic:
from typing import Any


def log(value: Any) -> None:
    print(value)
Overusing Any defeats the purpose of annotations. Treat it like unsafe in Rust: reach for it when necessary, not by default.


Callable
Functions passed as arguments can be typed:
from typing import Callable


def apply(func: Callable[[int], int], value: int) -> int:
    return func(value)


apply(lambda x: x * 2, 5)  # 10
Callable[[ArgType, ...], ReturnType] — the list contains parameter types, the second argument is the return type.


Generic Functions with TypeVar
TypeVar defines a placeholder type resolved at the call site, the same concept as a generic type parameter in Rust:
from typing import TypeVar

T = TypeVar("T")


def first(items: list[T]) -> T:
    return items[0]


first([1, 2, 3])  # return type inferred as int
first(["a", "b", "c"])  # return type inferred as str
Without TypeVar you would annotate the return as Any and lose the inference. With it, the type checker knows the return type matches whatever the list contains.


Protocol

Structural Subtyping

Protocol is Python’s formal answer to duck typing. It defines an interface by the methods a type must have, without requiring explicit inheritance. This is the closest Python analog to Rust traits:
from typing import Protocol


class Drawable(Protocol):
    def draw(self) -> None: ...


class Circle:
    def draw(self) -> None:
        print("drawing circle")


class Square:
    def draw(self) -> None:
        print("drawing square")


def render(shape: Drawable) -> None:  # accepts anything with a draw() method
    shape.draw()


render(Circle())  # fine
render(Square())  # fine
Neither Circle nor Square inherits from Drawable. The type checker verifies structural compatibility at the call site. This is duck typing formalized: if it has the right methods, it qualifies.


Final and Literal
Final declares a constant — a value that should never be reassigned:
from typing import Final

MAX_RETRIES: Final = 3
Literal constrains a parameter to a specific set of values. The type checker rejects anything outside the set:
from typing import Literal


def set_direction(d: Literal["north", "south", "east", "west"]) -> None: ...


set_direction("up")  # type checker error






WarningAnnotations do not run at runtime



None of this affects execution. If you pass the wrong type at runtime, Python will not stop you — it will simply fail when an operation on the wrong type fails. Run mypy or configure pyright in your editor to get the errors before runtime.





Functions
def greet(name):
    print(f"Hello, {name}!")  # f-string: embed expressions in strings


def add(a, b):
    return a + b


# default arguments
def connect(host, port=8080, timeout=30): ...


# variable positional arguments
def total(*numbers):
    return sum(numbers)


total(1, 2, 3, 4)  # 10


# variable keyword arguments
def create_user(**fields):
    print(fields)  # {'name': 'alice', 'role': 'admin'}


create_user(name="alice", role="admin")
Functions are first-class objects. They can be stored in variables, passed as arguments, and returned from other functions.


Control Flow
# if / elif / else
if x > 0:
    print("positive")
elif x == 0:
    print("zero")
else:
    print("negative")

# for iterates over any iterable
for item in [1, 2, 3]:
    print(item)

for i in range(10):  # 0 to 9
    print(i)

for i, item in enumerate(["a", "b", "c"]):
    print(i, item)  # 0 a, 1 b, 2 c

# while
while x > 0:
    x -= 1
for in Python iterates over any iterable: lists, strings, dicts, files, generators, database cursors. There is no index-based loop by default; use enumerate when you need the index.


Comprehensions

Python’s idiomatic way to build collections

Comprehensions are a concise syntax for building a new collection by transforming or filtering an existing iterable. They are the Python equivalent of chaining .map(), .filter(), and .collect() in Rust, but written as a single inline expression.

List Comprehensions
The foundation. [expression for item in iterable]:
squares = [x**2 for x in range(10)]
# [0, 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64, 81]
Add an if clause to filter:
even_squares = [x**2 for x in range(10) if x % 2 == 0]
# [0, 4, 16, 36, 64]
The Rust equivalent, for comparison:
let even_squares: Vec<i32> = (0..10)
    .filter(|x| x % 2 == 0)
    .map(|x| x * x)
    .collect();


Dict Comprehensions
{key_expr: value_expr for item in iterable}:
words = ["hello", "world", "python"]
lengths = {word: len(word) for word in words}
# {'hello': 5, 'world': 5, 'python': 6}

# invert a dict
original = {"a": 1, "b": 2, "c": 3}
inverted = {v: k for k, v in original.items()}
# {1: 'a', 2: 'b', 3: 'c'}


Set Comprehensions
{expression for item in iterable} — curly braces without a colon:
names = ["Alice", "Bob", "alice", "ALICE"]
unique_lower = {name.lower() for name in names}
# {'alice', 'bob'}


Generator Expressions
Generator expressions look like list comprehensions but use parentheses. They are lazy: values are computed one at a time as they are consumed, not all upfront:
# list comprehension: entire list built in memory immediately
squares_list = [x**2 for x in range(1_000_000)]

# generator expression: one value computed at a time
squares_gen = (x**2 for x in range(1_000_000))
Use a generator expression when you only need to iterate once, or when you are passing the result directly to a function that consumes it:
total = sum(x**2 for x in range(1_000_000))  # sum drives the generator
largest = max(len(word) for word in word_list)
When a generator expression is the only argument to a function, the outer parentheses serve double duty as the function call, so you only need one pair.


Nested Comprehensions
A comprehension can contain multiple for clauses, flattening nested structure:
matrix = [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6], [7, 8, 9]]
flat = [n for row in matrix for n in row]
# [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9]
Read left to right: “for each row in matrix, for each n in row, yield n.” The order of the for clauses matches a hand-written nested loop exactly:
flat = []
for row in matrix:
    for n in row:
        flat.append(n)
More than two for clauses becomes hard to read quickly. A regular loop is usually clearer beyond that point.


When to Use Each Form







Form
Use when




List comprehension [...]
You need the full collection in memory, or will iterate it more than once


Generator expression (...)
You iterate once, or pass directly to sum, max, join, etc.


Dict comprehension {k: v ...}
Building a mapping from an iterable


Set comprehension {...}
Building a deduplicated collection


Regular for loop
Multiple statements per iteration, side effects, or early exits



Comprehensions are not just stylistic. Python optimizes them at the bytecode level: a list comprehension is measurably faster than an equivalent for loop with .append() because it avoids looking up the append attribute on every iteration.



Unpacking and Destructuring

Binding multiple names at once

Unpacking assigns multiple names from a sequence in a single statement. It is Python’s counterpart to Rust’s destructuring, though without exhaustive pattern matching. It appears constantly in idiomatic Python code.

Basic Sequence Unpacking
Any iterable on the right-hand side can be unpacked into names on the left:
x, y = (3, 4)
a, b, c = [1, 2, 3]
p, q = "hi"  # strings are iterable too: p = 'h', q = 'i'
The count of names must match the count of values, or you get a ValueError.


Swapping Variables
Unpacking makes the classic swap a one-liner — no temporary variable needed:
a, b = 1, 2
a, b = b, a  # a = 2, b = 1
Python evaluates the entire right-hand side first (producing a tuple (2, 1)), then assigns. There is no aliasing hazard.


Extended Unpacking with *
A starred name captures the remaining elements into a list. It can appear at the start, middle, or end:
first, *rest = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]  # first=1,  rest=[2, 3, 4, 5]
*init, last = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]  # init=[1, 2, 3, 4],  last=5
a, *middle, b = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]  # a=1,  middle=[2, 3, 4],  b=5
The starred name always receives a list, even when zero elements match:
first, *rest = [42]  # first=42, rest=[]


Unpacking in for Loops
Any iterable of sequences can be unpacked directly in the loop variable:
pairs = [(1, "one"), (2, "two"), (3, "three")]

for number, word in pairs:
    print(number, word)
Dict .items() is the most common real-world case:
data = {"a": 1, "b": 2}

for key, value in data.items():
    print(key, value)
This is also why enumerate and zip feel so natural — their output is a sequence of tuples, designed to be unpacked:
for i, item in enumerate(["a", "b", "c"]):
    print(i, item)  # 0 a, 1 b, 2 c

for left, right in zip([1, 2, 3], ["x", "y", "z"]):
    print(left, right)  # 1 x, 2 y, 3 z


Nested Unpacking
Unpacking mirrors the shape of the data, however deeply nested:
(x1, y1), (x2, y2) = (0, 0), (3, 4)

segments = [((0, 0), (1, 1)), ((2, 2), (3, 3))]

for (x1, y1), (x2, y2) in segments:
    print(x1, y1, "->", x2, y2)


Unpacking into Function Calls
* and ** unpack sequences and dicts into positional and keyword arguments at the call site. This is the mirror image of *args / **kwargs in a function definition:
def add(a, b, c):
    return a + b + c


args = [1, 2, 3]
kwargs = {"a": 1, "b": 2, "c": 3}

add(*args)  # same as add(1, 2, 3)
add(**kwargs)  # same as add(a=1, b=2, c=3)
Both can be mixed with literal arguments:
def f(a, b, c, d): ...


f(1, *[2, 3], d=4)  # a=1, b=2, c=3, d=4
This is useful when arguments are built programmatically — for example, when forwarding arguments from one function to another, or constructing a call from a config dict.


The Walrus Operator :=
The walrus operator assigns a value and simultaneously returns it as an expression. It lets you assign inside a condition or comprehension without a separate statement:
# without walrus: the readline call must be duplicated
line = file.readline()
while line:
    process(line)
    line = file.readline()

# with walrus: assign and test in one expression
while line := file.readline():
    process(line)
In comprehensions it avoids computing an expensive value twice:
# expensive(x) is called twice for every element that passes the filter
results = [expensive(x) for x in data if expensive(x) > 10]

# walrus computes it once and reuses the result
results = [y for x in data if (y := expensive(x)) > 10]






NoteWhere := is allowed



The walrus operator is intentionally restricted to expression contexts: while conditions, if conditions, and comprehension filters. It cannot be used as a plain statement — that is what = is for. The restriction prevents it from replacing regular assignment, keeping the two visually distinct.

title: Python
text:
Reference Semantics and Memory
This section is the Python equivalent of the Memory Management section in the Rust chapter. Python hides the mechanics, but understanding them prevents a whole class of bugs that are otherwise very hard to track down.

Everything Is a Heap Object
In C, int x = 5 allocates four bytes on the stack. In Python, x = 5 creates an int object on the heap and binds the name x to it. Every Python value — integers, strings, functions, classes — lives on the heap. The interpreter manages all of it.
The variable x is not a box containing a value. It is a name in a namespace dictionary that points to an object. This distinction matters.


Assignment Copies the Reference, Not the Object
a = [1, 2, 3]
b = a  # b points to the SAME list object
b.append(4)

print(a)  # [1, 2, 3, 4] — a is affected
This is not a copy. Both a and b are names bound to the same list. The list has one identity and two names. Modifying the list through either name modifies the one shared object.
For comparison, the Rust equivalent would be a compile error: the borrow checker would reject two mutable references to the same data. Python has no such check; the aliasing is silent.
You can inspect identity with id() and the is operator:
a = [1, 2, 3]
b = a
print(id(a) == id(b))  # True: same object in memory
print(a is b)  # True: `is` checks identity, not equality
print(a == b)  # True: `==` checks value equality


Mutable vs Immutable Types
The behavior of assignment depends on whether the type is mutable or immutable.
Immutable types: int, float, bool, str, tuple, frozenset, bytes. You cannot change the object after it is created. Any operation that looks like modification creates a new object instead:
x = "hello"
y = x
x += " world"  # x is now bound to a NEW str object

print(y)  # "hello": y still points to the original
Mutable types: list, dict, set, bytearray, and most user-defined objects. The object can be modified in place, and all references see the change:
a = {"key": 1}
b = a
a["key"] = 99

print(b)  # {"key": 99}: same dict, one change visible through both names
This asymmetry is one of the most common sources of bugs for programmers new to Python. The rule to remember: assignment always copies the reference. For immutable types, this is safe because the object cannot change. For mutable types, it creates an alias.


Copying Mutable Objects
Three levels of copy:
import copy

original = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]

# 1. Alias: no copy at all
alias = original

# 2. Shallow copy: new container, same inner objects
shallow = original.copy()  # or list(original) or original[:]
shallow.append([5, 6])  # original unaffected: new container
shallow[0].append(99)  # original[0] IS affected: inner list is shared

# 3. Deep copy: new everything, recursively
deep = copy.deepcopy(original)
deep[0].append(99)  # original unaffected at every level
A shallow copy creates a new container but does not copy the objects inside it. If those objects are themselves mutable, the shallow copy shares them with the original. Deep copy recurses through the entire structure. For nested mutable data, the difference matters.


Identity, Equality, and Interning
is tests whether two names point to the same object. == tests whether two objects have equal values. They usually agree, but not always:
a = [1, 2, 3]
b = [1, 2, 3]

print(a == b)  # True: equal values
print(a is b)  # False: two distinct list objects
One exception worth knowing: CPython caches small integers (typically -5 through 256) and short strings that look like identifiers. These objects are reused rather than re-created, so is may return True even for separately created values in that range:
x = 42
y = 42
print(x is y)  # True in CPython: the integer 42 is cached

x = 1000
y = 1000
print(x is y)  # False: large integers are not cached
Never rely on this caching behavior. Use == to compare values and is only when you specifically mean to test object identity (most commonly: if x is None).


How Lists Allocate Memory
Python lists are dynamic arrays, similar to Vec<T> in Rust or std::vector in C++. They maintain an internal buffer that is larger than the current length, so that append is fast most of the time.
When the buffer is full and you append another element, Python reallocates: it allocates a new, larger buffer, copies the elements over, and frees the old one. The new capacity follows a growth formula that adds roughly one-eighth of the current size (plus a small constant for small lists). This gives a growth factor approaching 1.125 for large lists, smaller than Rust’s factor of 2 but still amortized O(1) per append.
You can observe the reallocation steps directly:
import sys

a = []
prev_size = 0
for i in range(20):
    a.append(i)
    size = sys.getsizeof(a)
    if size != prev_size:
        print(f"len={len(a):2d}  buffer size: {size} bytes")
        prev_size = size
The buffer grows in steps, not on every append. You pay for reallocation infrequently. If you know the final size in advance, a list comprehension avoids all intermediate reallocations by building the list in one pass:
# repeated append: may reallocate several times
result = []
for i in range(10000):
    result.append(compute(i))

# comprehension: single allocation, then fill
result = [compute(i) for i in range(10000)]


Dict and Set Internals
Dicts and sets are hash tables. Lookup, insertion, and deletion are O(1) average case. The hash table resizes when the load factor exceeds roughly two-thirds capacity, at which point it doubles in size. As with lists, this reallocation is amortized over many insertions.
Python dicts preserve insertion order as of Python 3.7. This is guaranteed by the language specification.


Reference Counting and Garbage Collection
CPython tracks a reference count on every object: the number of names and data structures that point to it. When the count drops to zero, the object is freed immediately and deterministically. This is similar in spirit to RAII in C++ or Rust’s ownership system, but managed automatically by the runtime.
import sys

a = [1, 2, 3]
b = a  # reference count is now 2
print(sys.getrefcount(a))  # 3 (getrefcount itself adds one temporarily)

del a  # count drops to 1: not freed yet
del b  # count drops to 0: freed immediately
Reference counting has one weakness: cycles. If object A holds a reference to object B, and B holds a reference back to A, neither count ever reaches zero, even if nothing else refers to them. CPython includes a separate cycle garbage collector that periodically detects and clears these cycles. It runs automatically; you rarely need to think about it.
The practical implication of reference counting: CPython’s memory release is more predictable than a generational GC. Objects are usually freed as soon as they go out of scope, not at some future collection point. This matters for resources like file handles and network connections: the with statement exploits this predictability.
with open("data.txt") as f:
    content = f.read()
# file is closed here, immediately, when the block exits


The Global Interpreter Lock
CPython has a Global Interpreter Lock (GIL): only one thread executes Python bytecode at a time. This makes CPython’s internals thread-safe without fine-grained locking, but it prevents true CPU parallelism across threads.
The practical implications:

I/O-bound work: threads work well. The GIL is released during I/O operations, so multiple threads can overlap network calls, file reads, and so on without blocking each other.
CPU-bound work: use multiprocessing (separate processes, each with their own GIL) or offload to C extensions like NumPy, which release the GIL for their inner loops.

Python 3.13 introduced an experimental free-threaded build (no GIL) as an opt-in option. It is not yet the default.


Memory-Efficient Patterns

Generators

A list comprehension builds the entire result in memory at once. For large or infinite sequences, a generator computes values lazily, one at a time:
# list comprehension: allocates all 10 million integers immediately
big_list = [x * 2 for x in range(10_000_000)]

# generator expression: allocates one integer at a time
big_gen = (x * 2 for x in range(10_000_000))


# generator function: same behavior, more control
def doubled(n):
    for i in range(n):
        yield i * 2  # suspends here, resumes on next iteration


for value in doubled(10_000_000):
    process(value)  # only one integer in memory at a time
The yield keyword turns a function into a generator. Its local state is suspended between calls and resumed on the next iteration. Generators are the idiomatic way to handle large data streams, infinite sequences, and processing pipelines without holding everything in memory.

title: Python
text:
Data Structures

list

Dynamic Array

a = [1, 2, 3]
a.append(4)  # O(1) amortized
a.insert(0, 0)  # O(n): shifts all elements
a.pop()  # O(1): remove last element
a.pop(0)  # O(n): remove first (use collections.deque if you need this often)
a[1:3]  # [2, 3]: slice — creates a shallow copy of that range
len(a)  # O(1)
3 in a  # O(n): linear scan
Lists are heterogeneous: they can hold objects of different types, including other lists. In practice, homogeneous lists (all the same type) are far more common and perform better with libraries like NumPy.


tuple

Immutable Sequence

t = (1, 2, 3)
t[0]  # 1
# t[0] = 99        # TypeError: tuples do not support assignment
Use tuples for fixed-size collections of heterogeneous data (coordinates, a record, a function return with multiple values). Use lists for variable-length collections of homogeneous data. Tuples as dict keys work; lists do not (mutable objects cannot be hashed).


dict

Hash Map

d = {"name": "alice", "age": 30}
d["name"]  # "alice"
d.get("missing", "default")  # "default": no KeyError
d["new_key"] = 42  # insert or update
"name" in d  # True: O(1) membership test
del d["age"]

for key, value in d.items():
    print(key, value)


set

Hash Set

s = {1, 2, 3}
s.add(4)
s.discard(10)  # no error if missing (remove() raises KeyError)
3 in s  # True: O(1)

a | b  # union
a & b  # intersection
a - b  # difference
a ^ b  # symmetric difference


str

Immutable Unicode Sequence

s = "hello"
s.upper()  # "HELLO": returns a new string
s.split(" ")  # ["hello"]
s.startswith("hel")  # True
f"value is {x:.2f}"  # f-strings for inline formatting
", ".join(["a", "b", "c"])  # "a, b, c"
Strings are immutable. Concatenating in a loop (s += x) allocates a new string on every iteration. For building strings from many parts, collect into a list and join at the end:
parts = []
for item in data:
    parts.append(str(item))
result = ", ".join(parts)  # one allocation

title: Python
Python
text:
Classes and Objects
class Point:
    def __init__(self, x, y):  # constructor
        self.x = x  # instance attributes
        self.y = y

    def distance_from_origin(self):
        return (self.x**2 + self.y**2) ** 0.5

    def __repr__(self):  # string representation for debugging
        return f"Point({self.x}, {self.y})"

    def __eq__(self, other):  # equality operator
        return self.x == other.x and self.y == other.y


p = Point(3, 4)
print(p.distance_from_origin())  # 5.0
print(p)  # Point(3, 4)
self is explicit: Python does not inject it invisibly. Every instance method takes self as its first parameter, giving you a clear signal that the method operates on the object.

Dunder Methods

The object protocol

Dunder methods (double underscore on both sides: __init__, __len__, __iter__, etc.) are how Python objects hook into the interpreter’s built-in operations. When you write len(obj), Python calls obj.__len__(). When you write for x in obj, Python calls obj.__iter__(). When you write with obj, Python calls obj.__enter__(). The built-in syntax is a thin layer over these methods.
This is what duck typing means at the implementation level: an object is a sequence if it has __len__ and __getitem__. An object is iterable if it has __iter__. The type hierarchy matters far less than the protocol an object implements.

String Representation
Two dunders control how an object is displayed:








Method
Used by
Purpose




__repr__
repr(obj), debugger, {obj!r}
Unambiguous; ideally valid Python to recreate the object


__str__
str(obj), print(obj), f"{obj}"
Human-readable display



class Point:
    def __init__(self, x, y):
        self.x = x
        self.y = y

    def __repr__(self):
        return f"Point({self.x}, {self.y})"  # looks like a constructor call

    def __str__(self):
        return f"({self.x}, {self.y})"  # friendlier display


p = Point(3, 4)
print(repr(p))  # Point(3, 4)
print(p)  # (3, 4)  — print calls __str__
If you only implement one, implement __repr__. Python falls back to it when __str__ is absent.


Operator Overloading
Arithmetic and comparison operators map directly to dunders:
class Vector:
    def __init__(self, x, y):
        self.x = x
        self.y = y

    def __add__(self, other):
        return Vector(self.x + other.x, self.y + other.y)

    def __mul__(self, scalar):
        return Vector(self.x * scalar, self.y * scalar)

    def __rmul__(self, scalar):
        return self.__mul__(scalar)  # makes 3 * v work, not just v * 3

    def __eq__(self, other):
        return self.x == other.x and self.y == other.y

    def __repr__(self):
        return f"Vector({self.x}, {self.y})"


v = Vector(1, 2)
print(v + Vector(3, 4))  # Vector(4, 6)
print(v * 3)  # Vector(3, 6)
print(3 * v)  # Vector(3, 6) — via __rmul__
When Python evaluates a + b it first tries a.__add__(b). If that returns NotImplemented, it tries b.__radd__(a). The reflected methods (__radd__, __rmul__, etc.) are how you make your type work on either side of the operator.
Common operator dunders:



Operator
Dunder
Reflected




+
__add__
__radd__


-
__sub__
__rsub__


*
__mul__
__rmul__


/
__truediv__
__rtruediv__


//
__floordiv__
__rfloordiv__


%
__mod__
__rmod__


**
__pow__
__rpow__


==
__eq__



<
__lt__



<=
__le__










Note__eq__ and __hash__



If you define __eq__ without defining __hash__, Python sets __hash__ to None, making the object unhashable — it cannot be used as a dict key or set member. Either define both, or use @dataclass(frozen=True), which handles both automatically.




The Container Protocol
Implement these to make an object behave like a sequence or mapping:
class Countdown:
    def __init__(self, start):
        self.data = list(range(start, -1, -1))

    def __len__(self):
        return len(self.data)  # len(obj)

    def __getitem__(self, index):
        return self.data[index]  # obj[i] and slicing

    def __contains__(self, value):
        return value in self.data  # `in` operator


c = Countdown(5)
print(len(c))  # 6
print(c[0])  # 5
print(3 in c)  # True
If you implement __getitem__ with integer indices starting at 0, Python will allow for x in obj to work automatically by repeatedly calling __getitem__ with increasing indices. It is cleaner to implement __iter__ explicitly.


The Iteration Protocol
for x in obj calls iter(obj) to get an iterator, then calls next() on it repeatedly until StopIteration is raised. You can implement this in two ways.
Option 1: The object is its own iterator. Implement both __iter__ (returns self) and __next__ (returns the next value or raises StopIteration):
class CountUp:
    def __init__(self, limit):
        self.limit = limit
        self.current = 0

    def __iter__(self):
        return self

    def __next__(self):
        if self.current >= self.limit:
            raise StopIteration
        value = self.current
        self.current += 1
        return value


list(CountUp(4))  # [0, 1, 2, 3]
The downside: iterating the same object twice picks up where the first left off. The state is shared.
Option 2: Return a fresh iterator from __iter__. The collection and the iterator are separate objects, so multiple independent loops work correctly:
class NumberRange:
    def __init__(self, start, stop):
        self.start = start
        self.stop = stop

    def __iter__(self):
        return iter(range(self.start, self.stop))  # fresh iterator each time
For complex iteration logic, a generator inside __iter__ is the most readable approach:
class EvenNumbers:
    def __init__(self, limit):
        self.limit = limit

    def __iter__(self):
        for n in range(0, self.limit, 2):
            yield n  # __iter__ becomes a generator; no __next__ needed


__call__
__call__ makes an instance callable like a function. This is the mechanism behind classes used as decorators:
class Multiplier:
    def __init__(self, factor):
        self.factor = factor

    def __call__(self, x):
        return x * self.factor


triple = Multiplier(3)
triple(7)  # 21 — called like a function


__bool__ and Truthiness
if obj: calls bool(obj), which calls __bool__. If __bool__ is absent, Python falls back to __len__: an object with length zero is falsy:
class Bag:
    def __init__(self, items):
        self.items = items

    def __len__(self):
        return len(self.items)


if not Bag([]):
    print("empty")  # prints: empty


Context Managers from the Inside
with obj as x: calls obj.__enter__() on entry (binding the return value to x) and obj.__exit__() on exit, whether or not an exception was raised:
import time


class Timer:
    def __enter__(self):
        self.start = time.perf_counter()
        return self  # this is what `as t` receives

    def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc_val, exc_tb):
        elapsed = time.perf_counter() - self.start
        print(f"elapsed: {elapsed:.4f}s")
        return False  # False: let exceptions propagate


with Timer():
    sum(range(1_000_000))
# elapsed: 0.0187s
__exit__ receives the exception type, value, and traceback if an exception occurred, or None for all three if the block exited cleanly. Returning True suppresses the exception; returning False or None lets it propagate.
For simpler cases, contextlib.contextmanager turns a generator into a context manager without writing a class:
from contextlib import contextmanager


@contextmanager
def timer():
    start = time.perf_counter()
    yield  # body of the with block runs here
    print(f"elapsed: {time.perf_counter() - start:.4f}s")


with timer():
    sum(range(1_000_000))
